title: Lyrical Ballads
alternative_titles: Lyrical Ballads, with a Few Other Poems
description: A small anonymous volume of twenty-three poems issued in the autumn of 1798 by two friends then living in the southwest of England. The supernatural narrative ballad that opens the book is by one hand and most of the shorter lyrics, tale-poems and conversation pieces by the other, so that the volume is an experiment in two related manners rather than a single voice. Its programme - later stated in the Preface of 1800 - was to treat incidents and situations from humble and common life in language really used by men, with a colouring of imagination that would give the appearance of novelty to familiar things.
plot_or_argument: The poems fall into three loose kinds. Long narrative ballads of guilt and penance supply the volume's emblem: a mariner kills an albatross gratuitously, is struck by a curse that leaves him the only survivor of his ship's company, and is condemned to tell his tale to each stranger he meets until the pain of the telling passes into love for all created things. Shorter tale-poems observe madness, destitution and superstition without moralising, letting an unreliable or agitated speaker make the story as he reports it. A third group of brief conversation lyrics and dialogues - a child who insists she is still seven although two of her siblings are dead, an old soldier and his solitary labour, a mother and her infant in the woods - locate moral instruction in the voice and the situation rather than in the poet's comment. The organising principle is therefore not plot but a stated policy of subject and diction.
narrative_structure: An anonymous collection rather than a designed sequence, with no frame narrative; the arrangement is rhetorical, opening on the long Romantic ballad, passing through tale-poems and dramatic dialogues, and closing on short meditative lyrics. Individual structures carry the diversity: the Mariner's tale-within-a-tale with its marginal gloss, monologues addressed to an overhearer, and single-voice conversation poems.
principal_characters: The Ancient Mariner; the Wedding-Guest; the Pilot and his son; Martha Ray of the thorn; the Mad Mother and her infant; the child who maintains that she is seven; Simon Lee and his young neighbour; Goody Blake and Harry Gill
literary_form: Lyrical ballad and popular-stanza narrative, together with the conversation poem and the dramatic dialogue; the volume draws on the revived antiquarian ballad tradition of the 1790s while abandoning its artificial diction.
meter_and_prosody: Principally the common metre and short ballad stanza of nursery and popular song, sometimes deliberately roughened and sometimes irregularly truncated; the long ballad uses an archaic eight- and nine-line stanza with a repeating refrain-word, the dialogue poems use plain blank verse or couplet-adjacent quatrains, and the meditative pieces are in unrhymed iambic pentameter.
historical_context: Composed in the years following the disappointment of the English hope raised by the French Revolution, during a retirement on Exmoor and in the Welsh and western borders, when an antiquarian ballad revival had already made popular stanza forms respectable again. The anonymous first edition was reviewed as the work of a single author and attacked for its meanness of subject and its prosaic diction, which drew out the explicit apology of the next edition's Preface.
literary_significance: Conventionally taken as the opening act of the English Romantic period, and the practical demonstration of a poetics of ordinary speech, humble life and imaginative colouring. Its ballads made the supernatural tale and the rustic conversation poem central to Romantic verse, and its theory of feeling recollected in tranquillity became the most quoted account of how poems are made.
attribution_notes: Issued anonymously and at first reviewed as a single author's work; the division of poems between the two contributors is settled by their later collected editions, in one of which the Mariner's ballad was placed under a separate head with its own explanatory note.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1798, in a small octavo volume for J. and A. Arch, anonymously; the volume was printed in Bristol. A second edition, containing few poems of the first and a long Preface, followed in 1800, a third in 1802 with an enlarged Preface, and the collaborators' poems were separated in their own collected editions thereafter.

title: Preface to Lyrical Ballads
alternative_titles: Preface to the Second Edition of Lyrical Ballads
description: The critical essay prefixed to the second edition of the ballad volume, greatly enlarged for the edition of 1802, and reprinted ever since as the founding document of English Romantic poetics. It defends a deliberate choice of humble and rustic life and of the language really used by such men, defines poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings originating in emotion recollected in tranquillity, and argues that the poet's distinguishing faculty is imagination rather than a conventional vocabulary of ornament. The essay also gives a polemical sketch of the diction of much eighteenth-century verse and a critical account of metre.
plot_or_argument: The argument moves from the choice of subject to the choice of language, then to a psychology of composition, a definition of the poet, and a polemic against poetic diction. Humble life is preferred because its feelings are simpler, more permanent and better understood by the people who speak them, so that ordinary speech is more philosophical than the substituted vocabulary of abstractions and personifications which passes for poetry; the poet, though a man speaking to men, is described as endowed with more lively sensibility and a larger knowledge of human nature. Composition is then analysed as recollection: the poem begins in emotion remembered, is contemplated until the mind creates in itself an analogous feeling, and is delivered over to metre, which supplies a proportioned part of pleasure and acts as a restraint on the pain of passionate subjects. The closing sections defend the experiments of the volume, rebuke the reader's appetite for trite ornament, and claim that the most valuable poet is he who gives most pleasure to the most people.
narrative_structure: A continuous discursive essay rather than a sequence of aphorisms: a statement of purpose, an argument for rustic subject and plain language, an account of the mental process of composition, a definition of the poet, and a polemic against current diction, with illustrative reference to particular poems in the volume and to Greek, Elizabethan and eighteenth-century practice.
literary_form: Prefatory literary commentary and theoretical essay in the tradition of the apologia dedicated to a published collection; it functions as a manifesto because it names the errors it intends to correct and proposes subjects and a style in their place.
meter_and_prosody: Prose in long argumentative periods, deliberately free of ornament and of the Latinate manner of eighteenth-century critical prose, though the essay analyses verse closely and its own rhythm is that of earnest exposition.
historical_context: Written in response to hostile reviews of the anonymous 1798 volume and to the taste for polished diction inherited from the later eighteenth century; the enlarged text of 1802 absorbed the criticisms of the experiments. Its ideas were inseparable from the collaboration and later disagreement with the co-author of the volume, whose own literary autobiography and criticism are in part a reply to it.
literary_significance: The most influential English statement of Romantic literary theory and the source of two of the period's most quoted formulas for the origin of poetry and for the poet's character. Its insistence that ordinary speech can be the medium of serious verse licensed the diction of later nineteenth-century poetry, and its account of imaginative perception remains the standard starting point for discussion of Romantic theories of the mind.
attribution_notes: Attribution is uncontested to the essayist of the volume's senior hand, with an acknowledged share for the co-author in the paragraphs on poetic metre; the texts of 1800 and 1802 differ, and scholarly editions print both.
bibliographical_notes: First printed London, 1800, prefixed to the second edition of the ballad volume; much enlarged in the edition of 1802 and reprinted with it thereafter. It has been separately edited many times, most fully in the apparatus of the modern collected critical work, and also appears in standard anthologies of literary criticism.

title: Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey
alternative_titles: Tintern Abbey
Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey, on Revisiting the Banks of the Wye during a Tour, July 13, 1798
description: The great blank-verse meditation of the early Romantic period, written at the close of a walking tour of the Wye valley and printed as the closing poem of the 1800 edition of the ballad volume. The speaker revisits a stretch of river-bank and steep woodland after five years and asks what the remembered landscape has actually done for his mind. The poem therefore moves from precise description to a history of three successive relations to nature, and ends as an address to his companion.
plot_or_argument: The speaker names the scene - the steep woods, the pastoral cliffs, the hedgerows, the winding river and the dwelling-places of hermits and of cottages - and insists that he sees them again as a living presence, not merely as a picture. He then reports what has happened in the interval: in earlier boyhood the delights of the landscape were animal and unthinking; in a later period they passed into trances in which the senses seemed half created to their proper office and the eye was lost in the hearing; and now, at a mature stage, there is added a sense sublime of something far more deeply interfused in the light of settings suns, the deep ocean, the air and the sky, which presses into the heart of man and moves all things that think and move. From this he learns to look on nature not as in the hour of thoughtless youth but hearing, sometimes, the still sad music of humanity, and finding in it a reward for former ceaseless wanderings. The poem closes by turning to his companion, in whom he sees what he once was, and praying that she will find the same binding influence in her future life, because nature never did betray the heart that loved her; she is addressed as the anchor of his purest thoughts and the guardian of his heart.
narrative_structure: A single continuous meditation in one voice, organised as a movement from present perception through remembered stages of the mind to a benediction addressed to another person; the topographical frame - the naming of the place, the date, the companion - is abandoned as the argument deepens and resumed in the closing lines.
principal_characters: The meditating speaker; his sister, walking with him on the bank; the absent companions of his former wanderings in the same valley
literary_form: Nature lyric and meditation in meditative blank verse; it transforms the eighteenth-century topographical and estate poem into an inward history of perception, retaining the local naming but abandoning the picturesque tour's habits of description.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter in a single continuous flow of 159 lines; the verse is built on the sentence rather than the stanza, with elastic syntax, delayed predicates and a heavy use of semicolon and colon, and lines of the most varied pause-pattern to imitate the movement of recollected thought.
historical_context: Composed in July 1798 at the end of a tour of the Wye valley, in the months before the poet's marriage and his settlement in the north-west, when the ruined abbey and its wooded valley were already a standard object of the picturesque tour. Its account of a philosophic mind formed by landscape answers both the picturesque verse of the previous generation and the associationist psychology then current.
literary_significance: The central text of the Romantic meditation and the canonical instance of the idea that landscape is given to the mind in stages, so that later readers have quoted it as the period's fullest account of how nature is known. Its phrases for the music of humanity and for nature's faithfulness are among the most quoted in English, and it is the standard test case for readings of memory, loss and the growing mind.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is printed from the working manuscript draft and from the 1800 text, and its title varies in the manuscript tradition, which is recorded in modern editions.
bibliographical_notes: Composed July 1798 and first printed London, 1800, in the second edition of the ballad volume, which was issued in January of that year; the draft was later used as the opening of the philosophical poem on the growth of the mind that remained unpublished in the author's lifetime, and the final text is recorded in the collected poetical works.

title: The Thorn
description: The most radical experiment of the anonymous 1798 volume: a long dramatic ballad narrated by a garrulous old man who reports what he thinks he has seen and heard on a hill where a thorn, a heap of moss and a nameless woman in a scarlet hood have gathered a local legend. The poem's interest is not the story but the mind of the teller - his superstition, his vanity, his need for a pathetic tale and his uneasy awareness that the simple truth would not serve him. A prose note explaining the narrator's character was appended in the edition of 1800, and the poem became the test case for the theory of poetic language defended in the Preface.
plot_or_argument: The narrator bids his listener open his eyes wide and observe the thorn, which looks older than it is, and the mound of moss, which looks like a grave though none lies there. He then reports the gossip of the neighbourhood: a woman named Martha Ray met her lover by that thorn, was deserted, and has ever since sat there with her hood about her face, calling on the name Edward in a voice that has frightened those who pass at night. He alternately insists on and disowns the tale, offering natural explanations, then abandoning them for the pleasure of the wonderful, and the poem ends on the repeated cry as it sounds in his own superstitious ear. The subject is thus the growth of a legend and the creative power of an uneducated and sorrowful mind, together with the pleasure a tale of woe can give when it is badly told.
narrative_structure: A dramatic monologue addressed to an overhearer, in stanzas of unequal length: description of the site, report of the local story, self-correction and protestation of honesty, and a final reversion to the repeated cry. The narrator's unreliability is the structure, since each stanza qualifies the one before it.
principal_characters: The aged, decayed and superstitious narrator; Martha Ray; the lost lover, Edward; the villagers whose gossip forms the legend
literary_form: Lyrical ballad and early form of the dramatic monologue; a poem that treats the popular tale as something made by the mind that tells it, and that places the psychology of belief in the foreground.
meter_and_prosody: A mixture of four- and three-beat ballad lines in stanzas of uneven length, marked by heavy punctuation, exclamatory emphasis and the repetition of words and half-lines, designed to imitate an excited and untrained voice rather than to sound poetical.
historical_context: Written in the period of the western collaboration, when the two poets were experimenting with the speech of persons whose language is less refined than that of the class of readers to whom it is addressed. The explanatory prose note of 1800, in which the narrator is accounted for by decayed fortune and superstitious habits rather than by rustic charm, is one of the first applications of the new theory to a particular text.
literary_significance: Taken by later critics as the clearest demonstration of Romantic interest in the unreliable imaginative narrator and in the psychology of belief, and an ancestor of the Victorian dramatic monologue. It is also the poem against which the co-author of the volume later weighed the success of the Preface's theory, praising in it the power of an excited and credulous voice.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the prose note of 1800, which explains the character of the speaker, is by the same hand and is printed with the poem in scholarly editions.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the anonymous 1798 ballad volume and reprinted in the editions of 1800 and 1802, to which the explanatory prose note was added; subsequent revisions and the history of the text are recorded in the modern collected edition of the poet's work.

title: Michael
alternative_titles: Michael, a Pastoral Poem
description: A pastoral poem in blank verse, the longest narrative admitted to the ballad volume after 1798, which redefines pastoral as the serious representation of a yeoman family and its attachment to an inheritance of land. Michael, an upland shepherd, his wife and their only son are bound to the family holding by labour, duty and love; the boy is sent to service in a distant town to raise money to redeem a mortgage, is lost through a single act of dishonesty and shame, and Michael, dispossessed, is left to build a sheepfold of stones for the shepherd who will never use it. It is at once a domestic tragedy of inheritance and an argument for the moral dignity of peasant life.
plot_or_argument: Michael's little inheritance lies under a mortgage contracted to relieve a kinsman's distress, and his infant son Luke is the heir of his labour, trained in the shepherds' duties from childhood and given a stated covenant and a stone to set at the building of the fold. To redeem the land the boy is sent to service with a relative in London, where he falls into dissipation and forfeits money entrusted to him; ashamed, he flees, and news reaches the valley only that he has died in prison or vanished. The old man's grief is silent, his wife's is passionate and reproachful, and the land passes out of the family's hands. Michael nevertheless lays out and builds the sheepfold on the rising ground above his cottage, stone by stone, in the expectation of a use that will never come, and the poem ends on the unfinished work and the fold that remains as a memorial of faithful love.
narrative_structure: A single continuous narrative in blank verse, opened by the poet's address to the valley and to the old man, followed by slow domestic exposition, one turn of fortune in the city episode, and a closing scene of unfinished labour that serves as the poem's moral image.
principal_characters: Michael, the shepherd; Isabel, his wife; Luke, their only son; the kinsman whose distress brings the mortgage on the land; the relative in the town with whom Luke is placed
literary_form: Metrical tale and pastoral poem in blank verse; the eighteenth-century theme of rural depopulation and the deserted village is converted into a domestic tragedy of entailed land and of the covenant between a father and son.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter with a deliberate weight and slowness of period and frequent enjambment; the diction avoids poetical ornament and is modelled on plain speech, an achievement the poem's first readers singled out in commendation.
historical_context: Composed largely in the winter of 1799-1800, after the poet's settlement in the north-west, in a decade of enclosure, agricultural distress and renewed debate over the decay of the independent yeomanry inherited from Goldsmith. Its theory of land as a school of moral attachment answers both the sentimental peasant of the 1790s and the political economy of the same years.
literary_significance: The strongest single poem of the Lake group's claim that humble domestic life is a proper subject for serious verse, and a lasting example of tragedy without catastrophe, in which an unfinished act of love carries the pathos. Later readers have made it central to arguments about property, inheritance and the rural order, and it remains standard evidence for the practice implied by the Preface.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Written chiefly in 1799-1800 and first printed in 1800, thereafter given a place in later editions of the ballad volume and in the collected poetical works. The periodical of first appearance is not named here because the sources consulted do not settle it; the year of first publication, 1800, is certain.

title: The Solitary Reaper
description: A short lyric of four stanzas, suggested by a scene witnessed during a tour of the Highlands and written in November 1805, in which a peasant girl reaps and sings at the same time in a language the listening speaker cannot understand. The poem's force lies in the withheld meaning: because the sense of the song is unavailable, the speaker invents possible subjects for it, and then surrenders the guess to the sound itself. He carries that sound away as a possession of memory, and the lyric becomes one of the period's plainest demonstrations of what its own theory of recollection claimed for poetry.
plot_or_argument: The speaker tells the valley to be still for one girl's song and watches her single in the field, reaping and singing at once. Since he cannot know what she sings, he asks whether it is some natural sorrow, loss or pain that may be and may be again, or an old, sad and forgotten story of battles long ago, and declares that no nightingale in the forests of the Arabian sand, nor cuckoo-bird in the farthest Hebrides, could have broken the silence of the seas with a happier measure. The girl turns to her labour and the song continues while she binds the sheaves, and the speaker listens motionless until the music stops. In the last stanza he reports that when he had seen and heard no more of it, the music was in his heart and was felt long after it was heard no more, as he lay on a couch in solitude or on a vacant pensive mood - that is, the song is recovered only in memory, and the poem records that recovery.
narrative_structure: An occasional lyric moving through a single scene: apostrophe to the landscape, description, a speculative question about the song's meaning, and a retrospective stanza of remembrance, in which the interval between hearing and recalling constitutes the argument.
principal_characters: The solitary Highland reaper; the travelling listener who remembers her song
literary_form: Nature lyric and song, a lyrical ballad of the later and smoother manner; the poem thematises the relation between untranslated speech, music and memory, and is built as an illustration of the poet's own definition of composition.
meter_and_prosody: Four quatrains alternating four-beat and three-beat iambic lines with a rhyme scheme that gives the poem an unmistakable song-like regularity; the imperative openings and the repeated question give it the pattern of an air, deliberately unlike the broken stanzaic manner of the 1798 ballads.
historical_context: Suggested by an incident on the tour of Scotland taken with his sister in 1803 and composed in November 1805, in the years in which the short lyrics of the 1807 collection were being gathered and the philosophy of the growing mind was being worked out in the long autobiographical poem. The scene of an English listener before a Gaelic song answers the period's vogue for Highland song and its collections of translated airs.
literary_significance: The period's shortest and most quoted illustration of its account of poetry: an uncomprehended sound made permanent by memory, and a demonstration that Romantic lyric can take its subject from a failure of understanding. It was widely imitated and translated in the nineteenth century and remains a standard test case for discussions of lyric address and of the autonomous song.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the author's own note identifies the scene as heard among a solitary Highland valley, and no rival claim has been made.
bibliographical_notes: Composed November 1805; first published in the two-volume collected edition of the poet's works, London, 1807, under the heading assigned to songs and to the poems of the imagination, and printed in every collected edition since. Later prose notes and the text's revisions are recorded in the modern scholarly edition.

title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
alternative_titles: The Daffodils
description: A lyric of four stanzas comparing the poet to a lone cloud floating over a valley, who comes upon a host of golden daffodils beside the lake and beneath the trees. Written two years after the walk that suggested it, and revised after its first publication, it is the period's most familiar poem and a working model of its own poetic theory: an accidental sight, remembered at leisure, becomes a source of repeated pleasure. Its first printed form bore the title The Daffodils.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, wandering solitary as a cloud, sees suddenly a long belt of daffodils stretching along the bay, tossing their heads in a sprightly dance, countlessly many as the stars that line the Milky Way. He at first gives the sight no value, gazing without thinking of the wealth the show had brought him; the second part of the poem transfers the scene to the mind, where, on a couch in a vacant or pensive mood, the flowers flash upon the inward eye which is the bliss of solitude, and the heart fills with pleasure and dances with the daffodils. The argument is thus a demonstration that the richest gifts of nature are received afterwards, in recollection, and that the imagination stores sensible forms as a permanent possession.
narrative_structure: Two-part movement within a single lyric: the outward scene of 1802 told as an event in the past tense, then the inward scene of later hours, with the turn signalled by the contrast between the thoughtless gaze and the pleasure recollected.
principal_characters: The solitary speaker, figured as a cloud; the host of daffodils; the lake, the trees and the breezy bay
literary_form: Nature lyric and lyrical ballad of the collected manner; a short meditative lyric that makes the process of remembering its explicit subject.
meter_and_prosody: Four stanzas of six iambic lines, the first four of four beats and the last two of a shorter beat, with a strongly marked rhyme pattern; the regularity and the repeated gestures of the stanza give the poem the quality of an air.
historical_context: Suggested by an afternoon walk by Ullswater in April 1802, recorded in the same words by the poet's companion in her journal of the tour, and composed in 1804 for the collection of short lyrics published in 1807. The revised text, with its second stanza added and its phrasing heightened, belongs to the edition of 1815.
literary_significance: The most anthologised and most parodied lyric of the English Romantic period, and the shortest complete illustration of the theory of emotion recollected in tranquillity. Its image of the inward eye became a common property of Victorian and later discussion of imaginative memory.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the suggested wording and the incident were shared with the companion named in the journal, but the poem is uniformly assigned to the writer.
bibliographical_notes: Composed 1804; first printed London, 1807, in the two-volume collected edition of poetical works under the title The Daffodils, and reprinted in the revised form in the edition of 1815; the manuscript and journal draft are preserved among the family papers held in the library of the poet's former college.

title: Composed upon Westminster Bridge
alternative_titles: Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802
description: A single descriptive sonnet written on the morning passage over the Thames, when the city lay asleep and its houses, ships and temples appeared in the beauty of the morning. It is remarkable in the poet's work as a wholly urban sublime, and in the history of the English sonnet as one of the few lyrics of the period that praise a great city without moralising about it.
plot_or_argument: The opening declares that no touch of solemn beauty is greater than this, and that the city wears the splendour of the earliest morning as though it were a garment, the houses seeming asleep while the bright and glistening Thames flows at his own sweet will and cares nothing for the hearts that stir below. The steeples, the theatres and the temples glitter in the dawn pure and bright, the fields are open and the air is smokeless, and the speaker insists that the dulllest eye must feel the stillness and the mighty spectacle. The closing lines name the reason of the calm: the great heart of the city lies at rest, its thousand homes are yet asleep, and the awake multitude that will fill the shops with strength has not yet risen. The argument is a paradox inherited from Augustan descriptive verse and here reversed: the loveliest hour of the busiest city is that in which it does nothing.
narrative_structure: A compressed occasional lyric in sonnet form: statement of theme, sequential description of river, buildings and sky, an appeal to the reader's sensibility, and a closing restatement of the stillness observed.
principal_characters: The sleeping city of London; the Thames, rolling at his own sweet will; the passing observer on the bridge
literary_form: Romantic sonnet and descriptive topographical lyric; the poem applies the vocabulary of the picturesque and of the sublime to an urban scene rather than to mountain scenery.
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter in a Petrarchan-style sonnet with an irregular rhyme scheme that runs in the opening through interlocking and repeated sounds, making the form closer to Milton's English sonnets than to the fashionable Miltonic imitation of the day.
historical_context: Dated by its title to the morning of 3 September 1802, on the journey that took the poet and his sister from London towards Calais; it belongs to the cluster of early sonnets on public and topical subjects, and it was first printed several years later in the 1807 collected edition.
literary_significance: One of the most quoted short poems in the language and the standard instance of the Romantic urban sublime, much discussed for its stillness, its impersonality and its defiance of the wilderness as the only seat of greatness. It helped revive the English sonnet after its long eclipse in the mid-eighteenth century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Composed September 1802; first printed London, 1807, among the sonnets of the two-volume collected edition; the poem circulated earlier in manuscript, and it was quoted approvingly in a familiar letter of the period before appearing in print.

title: Intimations of Immortality
alternative_titles: Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood
The Great Ode
description: The poet's greatest ode and the central Romantic poem about the loss and recovery of imaginative vision, begun in the spring months of the early 1800s, completed in stages, and printed in 1807. Its speaker finds that the glory and the dream of childhood sight have fled, and seeks a reason for the decay that shall also console him; the answer is a Platonising myth that the soul comes to us from God and hither trails clouds of glory, so that the child is finest in the vision which the adult increasingly loses.
plot_or_argument: The opening stanzas complain that a glory has passed away from the earth, and that the same flowers and the same sight of the heavens bring to the grown man none of the rapture they gave the child, for whom a cloud or a tale could fill the eye with tears. The central stanzas set out the myth of pre-existence: our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting, the soul that is our life's star has had its setting elsewhere and comes from afar, trailing clouds of glory from God who is our home, so that the infant, newest come from that country of light, sees most, and the growing boy sees least, until the shades of the prison-house begin to show upon him and the man is bound to the light of common day. The later stanzas recover the loss: the visionary gleam is gone, but the poet may still draw power from what remains behind, may read in the meanest flower that blows thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears, and may thank the human heart, with its tenderness, its joys and its fears, for the pity and the endurance that make the sober year of mature life richer than the rapturous first hours of childhood.
narrative_structure: An irregular Romantic ode in stanzas of unequal length, moving from a general complaint about the loss of vision, through the pictures of the infant, the boy and the youth, to the philosophical myth and then to the turn of consolation; the design follows the movement of feeling rather than a logical argument, and the later stanzas lengthen and slow as reflection displaces description.
principal_characters: The adult speaker; the child, infant, boy and youth whose successive stages are traced; Nature, personified as the nurse and guide of the child's days
literary_form: Romantic ode in the reflective and meditative manner, drawing on the English Pindaric and on Platonic and Christian ideas of the soul, and on the period's taste for the philosophical meditation in verse.
meter_and_prosody: Stanzas of irregular length and varied line, running from four to six beats, with an elaborate recurring rhyme pattern and refrains; the later ode stanzas lengthen and slow, so that metre is used to mark the difference between the child's quick vision and the adult's meditative periods.
historical_context: Begun in 1802, in the months of the poet's engagement and of the sonnets on liberty and on public subjects, continued in 1803-04, and completed in 1806; the poem's philosophy of pre-existence and its account of the child drew on the Platonism current among the poets and critics of the day and on the associationist psychology then standard in education.
literary_significance: The most ambitious Romantic statement of the relation between childhood, memory and loss, and the poem from which the language of the child as father of the man and of the glory that has passed away entered general use. It set the terms for later Victorian and modern discussions of imaginative decay, and it is the touchstone for readings of the poet's philosophy of the mind.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Printed London, 1807, in the two-volume collected edition, where it appeared with a subtitle that names its subject as recollections of early childhood; the four opening stanzas had been composed earlier and circulated among friends in manuscript. Its textual history, and the disputed question of the order of composition, are recorded in the modern scholarly edition.

title: Resolution and Independence
description: A long narrative-and-mediation lyric recording a meeting with an aged leech-gatherer on a bare Highland moor in the winter of 1802, and the effect of that meeting on a mind troubled by fears of its own destiny. The poem is at once a picture of solitary labour and a debate within the speaker's own breast, in which the old man's uncomplaining endurance becomes a rebuke and a support. It is the clearest example of the conversation poem raised to the length and weight of meditation.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with weather and with the speaker's own agitated moods: after a storm and a shining morning the poet asks why, if nature's plan for the animal is content, human hope should be tortured by fear of the morrow, and dwells on the sad and anxious thoughts that have followed him from infancy. On the moor he encounters a very old man, bent and blind, who supports himself by gathering leeches from the pools with a staff and a light, labouring day after day without help from man or boy. The speaker addresses him twice, and the old man answers in a plain account of his means and of his patience, repeating the same words in the same manner; the poem ends with the charge to himself to be strong and resolute, and to be warned and healed by the simple sight of that unhelped old man, whom the speaker figures as a type appointed by providence to test and steady the wavering mind.
narrative_structure: A three-part design: an outdoor prelude of weather and of personal doubt, a central encounter written largely as dialogue and reported speech, and a closing application in which the figure is read as a vision or sent agent. The repetition of the old man's words at two points in the encounter is the structural hinge of the poem.
principal_characters: The aged leech-gatherer, blind and staff-supported; the solitary poet-speaker who questions him
literary_form: Conversation poem and meditative lyric on the model of the earlier dialogue with a rustic; the poem's argument is the recovery of the mind from dejection by the observation of endurance.
meter_and_prosody: A long series of short stanzas of mixed four- and three-beat iambic lines with an insistent rhyme pattern, the regularity being used to register the old man's unwavering repetition against the more agitated syntax of the opening meditation.
historical_context: Written in January 1802 immediately after a meeting recorded in the same terms in the journal kept by the poet's sister, during a winter of fear for his own future and of anxiety about the fate of the revolutionary hope of his youth; the leech-gatherer's trade reflects the medical demand of the day, and the poem belongs to the group of moor and road encounters made out of the walking tours of the north.
literary_significance: A central poem of the period's account of how another person's plain speech can repair the poet's own mind, and the most discussed instance of the Romantic representation of age, poverty and stoical labour. Later criticism has made it a test case for the questions of whether such a figure is observed or invented, and of what the poem's rhetoric does to the voice of the man it consoles itself with.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the companion sonnet addressed to the same encounter is sometimes printed with it.
bibliographical_notes: Composed January 1802 and first printed London, 1807, in the two-volume collected edition; it had been intended earlier for the ballad volume and was long advertised in a companion sonnet among the poet's manuscripts; the journal note of the meeting is preserved with the family papers.

title: The Prelude
alternative_titles: The Prelude, or, Growth of a Poet's Mind; An Autobiographical Poem
The Poem to a Friend
description: The most important long poem of the English Romantic period and the first substantial autobiographical poem in the language in blank verse: a self-analysis of the making of a poet's mind, begun in 1798, completed in a thirteen-book form in 1805, and extensively revised over the following decades. It was never published in the writer's lifetime and appeared posthumously in 1850 under a title chosen by his family and editors. Its plan belongs to a larger philosophical scheme that was never finished, of which the published Excursion was meant to form the middle part.
plot_or_argument: The poem leaves the city of the author's birth and travels north through the first mountain journeys of boyhood, and thereafter follows the growth of his mind by a series of formative episodes set down in the order of experience rather than of argument. The incidents include the stealing of a boat on a lake at night, when a peak rose up and seemed to follow him like a living creature; the long wait for the horses on a winter evening among the wild country of the northern roads; the years at the university, when the prescribed studies left the imagination to seek its own food abroad; the residence in France during the first years of the Revolution and the subsequent journey over the Alps, where the real object of the hoped-for renewal rose above him unrecognised; and the sights of London, its beggars, its prisons, its travelling shows and its unending crowd. Through all of these a sense of power, of a mind in union with the invisible world, is felt in the mountain and river scenery, and the poem's argument is that external nature, administered by a shaping spirit, educated the poet's imagination and affections, so that the poet is to be known by what his mind made of what he saw.
narrative_structure: An autobiographical poem in books of unequal length - thirteen in the version of 1805, fourteen in the posthumous text of 1850 - organised as a travel narrative of the mind: it alternates narrative episode, descriptive passage and sustained reflection, and is held together by a single addressing voice that looks backward across an interval of years and asks what those experiences have made.
principal_characters: The poet's own successive selves - the boy, the college student at Cambridge, the traveller in the Alps, the resident in revolutionary France and in London; Nature, addressed as a power that trains, disciplines and reassures the growing mind
literary_form: Autobiographical and philosophical poem in blank verse, a poet's mind in the shape of an epic without a hero's actions; it draws on the tradition of the contemplative and topographical poem and on the Romantic essay in psychological analysis.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter throughout, in a style of extraordinary flexibility, with long flowing periods, Latinate inversion and a deliberate abundance of general nouns, and frequent apostrophes to the mountains and to the powers of the mind.
historical_context: Conceived in 1798 as a philosophical poem to be built upon the account of the growth of the poet's mind, and revised in the years after the disappointment of the French Revolution and the settlement in the Lake District; the 1850 posthumous text, prepared after the author's death by members of his family, represents the later and more conservative revision and suppressed the more radical passages of the 1805 version, which was recovered by scholarship only in the twentieth century.
literary_significance: Founded the Romantic autobiographical poem and set the pattern of later long poems of the self's education; its phrase for the growth of the mind became the standard description of the lyric of memory, and its account of the imagination as a moral and perceptual power remains central in the history of ideas. The recovery of the 1805 text transformed the poet's reputation and made the poem's political and psychological passages matters of continuing argument.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the two distinct recensions of 1805 and 1850 are both by the same author, and modern editions print them in parallel with their revisions recorded.
bibliographical_notes: First published posthumously London, 1850, in fourteen books, in a volume of the poet's collected works and under the title assigned by his editors; the manuscript of the 1805 thirteen-book version, held among the family papers, was edited by scholars in the twentieth century and is now the basis of most teaching texts. The larger philosophical poem of which the work was planned as an introduction, and of which the Excursion forms the middle, was never executed.

title: The Excursion
alternative_titles: The Excursion. Forming a Part of the Recluse
description: The only completed and published portion of a great philosophical poem that was planned but never written, issued in 1814 as a single volume of blank verse in nine books and described on its title page as forming part of the larger work. It records a day's walk in the northern mountains with an aged pedlar, and the conversations the walk produces among the narrator, the Wanderer, a despondent Solitary and a country Pastor. Its subject is the condition of human hope, melancholy and belief, argued through competing voices rather than by a system.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, wandering among the hills, falls in with the Wanderer, an old pedlar of patient and cheerful mind, and with him ascends towards a hill community; at its edge they meet a Solitary, once a man of affairs and letters, whose hope for mankind has been wrecked by private losses and by the public history of the age, and who urges that the mass of the people are made miserable by institutions, by unequal wealth and by the course of the world. The Wanderer and the Pastor answer with the consolations of duty, of domestic affection, of labour, of the church and of the mind's intercourse with nature, and the middle books recount the lives of the humble dead of the village churchyard, each a small lesson in endurance. In the books set on and about the mountain height the Solitary is pressed but not converted, and the argument is carried forward rather than closed; the poem ends with the Pastor's meditations in the churchyard and with an invocation of evening and a defence of human hope against despondency, resting on the permanence of the moral law and on the strength lodged in the poor.
narrative_structure: A poem of nine books in dramatic-narrative form: an external journey through a single day in an identifiable mountain district, framed so that each stage releases a long set speech, with three principal speakers whose contentions answer one another; the narrator's reflective passages and the churchyard narratives bind the debates together.
principal_characters: The Wanderer, an aged pedlar of the hills; the Solitary, a disillusioned former man of business and letters; the Pastor, a country clergyman; the Narrator, the poet's own speaking voice; the humble dead of the churchyard, several of whose lives the Pastor commemorates
literary_form: Philosophical poem and conversational poem in blank verse, on the model of the didactic and contemplative poem; its one-day journey structure descends from the topographical tradition, while the set speeches belong to the Romantic debate about belief, consolation and social hope.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter throughout, in a stately and deliberately elevated manner, with long paragraphic speeches, elaborate punctuation, and occasional lyric and hymn-like interpolations of shorter metre, notably in the Pastor's narrative of the humble dead.
historical_context: Grown out of the plan of a philosophical poem announced in correspondence at the start of the century, composed in fits between 1802 and 1813, and published in 1814 as a detached part of a work whose rest never existed; its debates register the disappointment of the revolutionary hope of the 1790s, the condition of rural and manufacturing distress, and the poet's own movement towards a conservative national and ecclesiastical position.
literary_significance: The most substantial and most attacked long poem of the later Romantic period: reviewers received it as a proof of the failure of the system it served, and its fate discouraged the large philosophical poem in English for a generation. It nevertheless preserved the argument of the age about consolation, nature and social hope in a single continuous work, and its churchyard book has been central to recent accounts of Romantic mourning and of rural elegy.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1814, in a single volume by the long-standing publishers of the author's collected work, with a title page announcing it as forming a part of a larger poem; earlier portions of the design had appeared as separate short poems, and the intended scheme, and the parts never written, are documented in the author's correspondence and in modern editions.

title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
alternative_titles: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere
description: The long supernatural ballad that opens the anonymous 1798 volume and soon became the most discussed poem of the English Romantic period. A wedding-guest on his way to the feast is stopped by an old seafarer who tells how his ship drove south to the equator and the icy seas, how an albatross that had followed them through the fog was shot with a cross-bow, and how the guilt of that gratuitous act brought death on all hands but his own. The poem is a tale of penance as much as of adventure: the Mariner is condemned to live, to know what he has done, and to tell the story again to each stranger who seems to choose him for his listener.
plot_or_argument: The Mariner's ship is becalmed in a hot and rotting sea after the killing of the bird, and his crew, who first approved the deed and then lament it, are visited by a skeleton hull carrying two passengers, Death and Life-in-Death, who play a game for the ship's company. Two hundred men drop one after another and cannot bury their dead, while the Mariner alone survives, unable to pray and with the dead bird hung about his neck in place of the cross; the charm breaks only when, without meaning to, he blesses the water-snakes that coast the ship, and the albatross falls from his neck. He is then guided homewards by a spirit, and the tale of the killing and of the curse is told again, its moral delivered in the lines that say that he who loves all things that God made and made best prays best. The outer scene closes with the wedding-guest, from whom the Mariner departs, left like a stunned man and, in the poet's phrase, a sadder and a wiser man; the story has taught him to distrust his own joy and to value the created world.
narrative_structure: A framed oral narrative: an outer scene at the wedding-gate, an inner first-person confession divided into seven parts, and, when the poem was reprinted in 1817, an added marginal gloss in the manner of an old ballad or a commonplace book, which annotates and at times ironically moralises the tale. The frame returns in the closing stanza.
principal_characters: The Ancient Mariner; the Wedding-Guest; the Pilot and the Pilot's boy; the Hermit; Death and Life-in-Death; the albatross; the dead ship's company
literary_form: Lyrical ballad and metrical romance in verse, written in the revived manner of the antique minstrel ballad, with deliberate archaisms, and transformed into a vision of guilt, curse, repentance and the sacredness of created things.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly the ballad stanza of alternating four-beat and three-beat lines with a leading rhyme, varied by internal rhyme, alliteration, repetition of a single keyword and occasional shorter stanzas, giving an insistent song-like movement; archaic spelling and vocabulary were introduced to strengthen the impression of an old recovered tale.
historical_context: Composed principally in the spring and summer of 1798 during the western collaboration, and suggested in part by a shared reading of accounts of southern voyages; its theology of sin, curse and enforced penance belongs to the poem's moral imagination rather than to any single source. Its first readers were divided between admiration for its power and complaints that its diction and machinery were absurd.
literary_significance: The poem that established the Romantic supernatural ballad and made the outcast confessing narrator a permanent figure of modern verse; it supplied the period's most quoted image of unforgiven guilt and of the love owed to all created things. Its critical history, from the reviews of 1798 to the gloss of 1817 and to the poet's own later account of the volume's plan, is a classic case study of Romantic reception.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was contributed by the collaborator who later wrote the volume's critical history, was given a head of its own in the second edition, and was placed in a separate section of his collected poems in 1817.
bibliographical_notes: First printed London, 1798 (the volume was printed in Bristol), opening the anonymous ballad volume with the archaic title spelling; reprinted largely rewritten and with the added marginal gloss in the poet's volume of 1817, which is the basis of most modern texts, the 1798 reading being recorded in the apparatus.

title: Kubla Khan
alternative_titles: Kubla Khan: A Vision in a Dream. A Fragment.
description: A short visionary fragment published in 1816 with a prose account of its origin in a sleep induced by an anodyne on a west-country tour, when the poem is said to have risen entire in the dreamer's mind and to have been lost, except for a few hundred lines, through interruption by a person on business from the village. The poem sets the pleasure-dome of the Mongol emperor against the image of a poet able to recreate such a place in song, and ends in terror at the power of the inspired man.
plot_or_argument: The first movement decrees the stately pleasure-dome of Kubla Khan, with its gardens bright and its walls and towers, and the rivers that run with swift ecstatic friction through forests and measureless caverns to a sunless sea. The second movement turns to the deep romantic chasm that slanted down the green hill athwart a cedarn cover, wild with the woman wailing for her demon-lover, and to the fountain that rises in suspense, flinging up half-intermitted blocks and throwing logs and kottles into the labouring cavern, until the dome and the cavern-wonders are mingled in one hearing of the thunder of the waters. The closing movement abandons the description for the poet himself: could he revive within him the hollow and inspiring song of the Abyssinian maid, he would rebuild that dome and those caves of wonder, and his hearers, seeing the gleam and hearing the music, would fear and cry aloud at the sight; for the poet has fed on the paradise of the vision and drunk the milk of its divine woman. The argument is thus an image of the imaginative act, of the palace built in the air by the poet and of the terror that attends such power.
narrative_structure: A fragment in three movements of unequal length and without a completed argument: the scene of the dome, the chasm and its supernatural music, and the poet's visionary ambition, the transitions being made by sound and by image rather than by exposition.
principal_characters: Kubla Khan, the emperor who decrees the dome; the poet-speaker who would recreate the vision in song; the woman wailing for her demon-lover; the Abyssinian maid with her stringed instrument
literary_form: Visionary lyric and metrical romance in verse; a dream-poem in the line of the medieval vision, written as a study in the power of sound to carry what the argument cannot complete.
meter_and_prosody: Irregular accentual verse of exceptional richness, with lines running from two to six beats in a scheme of recurring rhyme, internal echo and repeated words, and a marked difference of pace between the flowing opening, the agitation of the chasm and the terror of the closing lines.
historical_context: Composed, on the author's own later account, in the years of the western collaboration and of the opium experiments that followed; the date has been debated on the evidence of the manuscript and of contemporaries who heard the poem read before the turn of the century, and it was printed at last in 1816 at the instance of a brother-poet then abroad.
literary_significance: The most celebrated fragment in English and a central text for all later writing on dream, intoxication and imaginative creation; its pleasure-dome and its caverns of measureless depth entered the language of literary and general discourse. It is also the most quoted example of the Romantic poem that makes the interruption of vision and the failure of memory its subject.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date and circumstances of composition are debated, reliance falling on the author's own 1816 preface and on the evidence of readers who heard the poem before 1800.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1816, in a small volume issued with a longer romance of the same hand and with a prefatory note on the dream origin of the fragment; the holograph manuscript and the copies made for friends before publication are the basis of the modern textual and biographical discussion.

title: Christabel
alternative_titles: Christabel: a Fragment
description: A long metrical romance in two incomplete parts, long circulated in manuscript and published in 1816, which tells how a knight's daughter walking alone at midnight in the woods about her father's castle meets a strange maiden, and how the household is changed by the stranger's presence. Its machinery belongs to the supernatural ballad and to the Gothic tale of enchantment, and its interest lies in an atmosphere of guilt, spell and dread rather than in an explained plot.
plot_or_argument: Christabel, unable to sleep, goes out at midnight to the terrace and the forest and meets a stranger who names herself Geraldine and says that she has been forced from her home and dragged through the wood by those who would compel her to a hated marriage; she asks shelter, and Christabel, bound by a spell that forbids her to question or to name the stranger's errand, leads her through the hall and to her own chamber. The intermediate lay, sung by the minstrel Bard Brice, tells how a dove, guarding a nest, was killed by a serpent that coiled about the shrub, and is heard as an omen of the wrong done in the castle. The second part brings the return of Lord Leoline, who had been absent on a border errand, the greeting of his hound, and the strange new affection that the stranger excites in him, while Christabel sees and may not tell what sits about the form she has brought within doors. The poem breaks off with the spell unbroken and the story unfinished, the promised conclusion never having been written.
narrative_structure: An unfinished romance in parts, organised as a series of set pieces rather than as continuous narrative: the midnight meeting, the chamber scene, the interpolated lay of the dove and the serpent, and the return of the father; the promised third part was never executed, and the poem's meaning has been much discussed as an enchantment of the household by a seducing power.
principal_characters: Christabel, the knight's daughter; Geraldine, the stranger maiden under a spell; Lord Leoline, her father; Bard Brice, the minstrel who sings the ominous lay; the mastiff of the hall
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, combining the supernatural ballad, the Gothic tale of the enchanted woman and the romance of the castle and its rites.
meter_and_prosody: A deliberately irregular accentual metre of lines of unequal beat, whose pattern is regulated by the number of accents rather than of syllables, with recurring rhyme-schemes that vary with the emotional register of each scene; the verse was cited by later critics as the first modern English example of accentual measurement.
historical_context: Begun in the years of the western collaboration and the ballad volume, the first part composed in the late 1790s and the second about 1800; its long circulation in manuscript made its reputation among the poet's friends before publication, and its appearance in print in 1816 coincided with a renewed public interest in tales of border and of enchantment.
literary_significance: One of the most imitated unfinished poems in English and a standard instance of the Romantic use of enchantment, guilt and suspense without explanation; its metre influenced the later lyricists of the period, and its fragmentary state has made it a permanent subject of textual and psychoanalytical reading.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the author's own later accounts assign the parts to different years of composition, and the dating of the promised conclusion remains a matter of inference.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1816, in a small volume issued with a shorter visionary fragment and with a prefatory note; manuscript copies of the two parts and the private printings made for friends before publication are recorded in modern editions.

title: Frost at Midnight
description: The most perfect of the conversation poems: a short blank-verse meditation written in a west-country cottage at night, where the speaker sits with his infant sleeping near him and the only visible motion is the film of frost that settles on the languid flame of his fire. Out of that stillness he argues that the mind creates its own moods from what it hears, recalls the school days when such silence and the few small sounds of an evening were all the variety he had, and ends with the hope that his child, reared among hills and lakes, shall learn his language from the eternal forms of nature.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins with the strange patience of the frost, which hangs on the fire-wood and performs its ministry in silence, and from that observation the speaker turns to the question of how the mind supplies its own sound, illustrating it by the listeners who borrow from themselves the melancholy or the comfort of an hour. He then recalls his own rearing in a great city, where nothing of the living seasons was visible and the eye found no familiar shapes of hill or field to which it could go in sympathy; all that variety was made for him by the changing sounds of evening, the flutter of a film on the fire, the note of a cricket or the hoot of an owl. In the closing movement he addresses the babe sleeping by its mother's side, and pledges that the child shall walk among the hills and the lakes, and shall see and hear the seasons as they change, and that nature, in every living thing, shall be a teacher to him; the poem ends with the confession of his own childhood's want and with the prayer that the eternal Beauty, which is present in all the forms of the world, shall be the child's guide and guardian.
narrative_structure: A single meditative movement in one voice, built as a sequence of retirements and returns: the outer stillness of the frost, the inward memory of the city and the school, the image of the sleeping infant, and the closing hope for the child's future education; the transitions are made by association rather than by argument.
principal_characters: The speaker alone in his cottage at night; his infant son, asleep in the cradle; the absent mother of the child; the school-hours and the town of the speaker's childhood
literary_form: Conversation poem and lyric meditation in meditative blank verse, the form in which the period replaced the Augustan imitation and the estate poem with a private scene of thought.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of exceptional quietness, with a high proportion of soft monosyllables, delayed predicates and suspended syntax, and long vowel music; the tempo of the line imitates the pace of a mind listening to its own silence.
historical_context: Written in the cold spring of 1798 in the cottage in which the collaboration of the ballad volume was beginning, and addressed to the first years of the poet's married life and to his infant son; its educational hope for the child answers the contemporary debate about schooling and about the formative influence of place, and it draws on the associationist psychology the poet had lately been reading.
literary_significance: The standard example of the Romantic conversation poem and one of the most quoted blank-verse meditations on childhood, education and the perception of nature. Its account of the mind's creation of its own mood, and its blessing on the child who is to learn from the living landscape, became common property of later nature writing and of Romantic pedagogy.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Composed 1798 and first printed in that year; the name of the periodical of first appearance is not restated here because the sources consulted leave it unsettled. The poem was collected in the volume of 1817 and its text, with the variations of the manuscript, is recorded in the standard edition.

title: Dejection: An Ode
alternative_titles: Dejection, an Ode
description: An occasional ode of the spring of 1802, written over some days in a season of despair over a love that could not be answered and over the poet's own loss of imaginative power, and addressed to a woman named in an earlier version of the text. It is the most explicit verse statement of the Romantic theory of perception, since its argument is that the passion we bring to a scene is the source of its worth, and that a mind which cannot feel gives nothing to what it sees. The storm that gathers outside the window, watched without emotion, is the emblem of the speaker's condition.
plot_or_argument: The opening invokes the evening wind, the last leaves that fall from the tree, and the storm gathering over the sea, and the speaker reports how he looks upon the face of the world with no sense of joy and no fear of loss, able neither to weep nor to sleep for want of feeling. Turning to the addressee, he says that grief without the imaginative power is a dumb and shapeless misery, and recalls that there was a time when the beauty of the world was attended by a holy light and by a joy too keen not to be painful. The central assertion is then laid down plainly: what we seem to receive from outward things is given and borrowed from ourselves, and the passion and the intelligence of the mind are the wedding garments of the world it beholds; a creature without imagination has no power to create or to enjoy. The closing stanzas return to the storm and to the prayer that the listener, whose life is bound to a household and to a child, may keep the fancy and the feeling that make the world fair, while the speaker accepts his own duller fate and asks only to be left to his silence and his penance.
narrative_structure: An irregular ode in eight sections, moving from the description of the storm, through the confession of impotence, to the philosophical assertion about the mind's agency, and back to the address to the listener; the design is that of a passionate self-analysis rather than of a close argument.
principal_characters: The speaker beneath the storm in his room; the addressee, a woman loved and unattainable, whose household is named in the poem; the wind, the clouds and the sinking moon of the opening
literary_form: Romantic ode and meditation in the conversation manner, combining the eighteenth-century irregular ode with the letter of apology and the poem of psychological analysis.
meter_and_prosody: Irregular ode stanzas of unequal line-length with a complex rhyme scheme and persistent exclamatory and interrogatory periods; the alternation of long storm lines and shorter reflective lines marks the alternation of feeling and argument.
historical_context: Written in April 1802, in a season of estrangement from his family, of increasing dependence on laudanum, and of hopeless attachment to a member of his wife's family; it belongs to the years in which his public lectures and his periodical were in difficulty, and its theory of the imagination was restated in prose in his critical work of 1817.
literary_significance: The classic Romantic poem on the failure of the imaginative faculty and one of the plainest statements of the mind-dependent view of perception; its claim that the mind supplies what it seems to receive from the world became a central tenet of Romantic theory. It remains a touchstone for readings of the relation between biography, intoxication and the Romantic ode.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the identity of the addressee is a matter of biographical inference and does not affect the question of authorship.
bibliographical_notes: Composed April 1802 and first printed later in the same year in a London newspaper; it was collected in the volume of 1817, where the title and the address were modified and the earlier personal passages removed, the first text being recorded in the modern edition.

title: The Eolian Harp
alternative_titles: The Aeolian Harp
Effusion, written at Clevedon, Somersetshire
description: The first and shortest of the conversation poems, written at Clevedon in the summer of 1795 in the months of the poet's courtship and first marriage, and printed among his earliest collected poems. An Aeolian harp, strung by the wind in a window-frame of the cottage, supplies the occasion: the speaker listens to its random music, lets his thoughts pass into a speculation on the one life and one intelligence that runs through all things, and is then drawn back, in the closing lines, by the voice of the woman beside him to duty and to a sober faith.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the description of the harp and of the breeze that plays over its strings, and with the reflection that such an instrument yields infinite variety to the attentive ear and seems to possess a faculty of its own. From this the speaker passes to the central speculation: if all animated nature were but a collection of sensitive instruments played upon by one intellectual and vital being, the whole of created life might be a member of one ever-living mind, and the sense of the beautiful and the sense of the holy would be one and the same feeling. The last part withdraws that fancy as an error of unassisted thought, and turns to the speaker's companion, whose gentle voice and hopes reprove the bewilderment of his soul; she is hailed as the guardian of a wiser and humbler virtue, and the poem ends with the prayer that her heart's affections, and the duties and the faith that belong to a life lived in domestic love, shall be the poet's portion.
narrative_structure: A single meditative movement in three parts, with the turn marked by an address to the listening woman: the outward scene of the harp and the sea, the speculative flight into the philosophy of one life, and the return to domestic duty and Christian modesty. The form gives the poem its characteristic air of a thought overheard and then corrected.
principal_characters: The speaker at his window; his companion and newly married wife, whose voice interrupts the speculation; the Aeolian harp and the evening breeze
literary_form: Conversation poem and lyric meditation in reflective blank verse, drawing on the eighteenth-century meditation upon a natural object and on the contemporary vogue for the Aeolian harp as a figure of the passive mind.
meter_and_prosody: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of continuous and softened movement, with long vowel music and suspended syntax in the speculative passage and shorter, plainer periods in the closing address; the poem is written as a single unbroken paragraph of meditative verse.
historical_context: Composed at Clevedon on the eve of the poet's marriage, at a time when associationist psychology and a nature-philosophy deriving from the German schools, with its idea of one life running through all things, were actively read in England; the Aeolian harp had become a fashionable emblem of sensibility and of the mind acted upon.
literary_significance: The founding text of the Romantic conversation poem and one of the earliest English lyrics to make the theory of the associative and passive mind the subject of a meditation. Its speculation and its self-rebuke have made it a standing case in discussions of pantheism, orthodoxy and the development of the poet's early thought.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was revised and its speculative passage abridged under the author's own hand in later collected editions, and the earlier and fuller text is printed in modern editions.
bibliographical_notes: Composed 1795; first published London, 1796, in the poet's earliest volume of poems, where it appeared among the short effusions; the several reprintings in which the pantheistic passage was altered are recorded in the standard collected edition.

title: Biographia Literaria
alternative_titles: Biographia Literaria; or, Biographical Notices of my Literary Life and Opinions
description: The central work of English Romantic literary criticism and theory, published in two volumes in 1817 and made up of the author's literary autobiography, his history of his own opinions, and a sustained analysis of imagination, fancy and symbol. It is famously miscellaneous, interrupting its own narrative with translations, psychological disquisition and quarrels, and it contains both the classic account of the Romantic theory of the imagination and the most searching criticism of the poems and the prefatory theory of the collaborator who had supplied the ballad volume's shorter pieces.
plot_or_argument: The book moves between three kinds of matter. First, a memoir of the author's education, his communitarian scheme on the American frontier, his residence in Germany and his first lectures, which supplies the account of a mind formed by books and by disappointment. Second, a philosophical criticism which distinguishes fancy from imagination, describes the primary imagination as the living power and prime agent of all human perception, repeats the echo of that infinite act in every finite mind, and gives the secondary imagination as an echo of the former, coalescing with the objects of its contemplation and dissolving, diffusing and re-creating in order to idealise; symbol is defined as that which partakes of the reality of the thing it conveys. Third, a critical history of the ballad volume, in which the prose romances of the author's own hand are said to aim at the willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith, and in which the theory and the practice of the collaborator's verse are examined with admiration and with reproach, the famous chapters on the philosophy of the mind being at once an exposition and a quarrel.
narrative_structure: A two-volume miscellany following no single order: autobiography, translation, philosophical dissertation and practical criticism alternate, and the book repeatedly breaks off its own story, the author's apology for its desultory plan forming part of its design; whole chapters were withdrawn or recast in the reprintings.
principal_characters: The author as the memoirist of his own opinions; the friend and collaborator whose theory and verse are examined; the German philosophers and the English critics whose texts and doctrines are translated, quoted or answered
literary_form: Critical treatise and literary autobiography, in the line of the formal miscellany of the period; it combines memoir, philosophical psychology and practical criticism in a single discursive work.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of great density and range, passing from the plain autobiographical sentence to the Latinate periods of the philosophical chapters; the style of the book, with its coinages and its vocabulary of perception, became itself a model for English critical writing.
historical_context: Written out of the author's London lecturing years and his residence in Germany, where he had read the transcendental philosophy, and published in the year of his collected poems, when the reputation of the Lake school was being made and attacked in the reviews; the book's history of the ballad volume is also a defence of his own share in it, and one of its chapters was withdrawn when its dependence on a German source was challenged.
literary_significance: The most quoted body of theory in English Romantic criticism, and the source of the standard distinctions between fancy and imagination, of the definition of symbol, and of the phrase for the willing suspension of disbelief. Its account of perception and creation has governed later reading of Romantic poetry, and its mixture of memoir, philosophy and polemic defines the Romantic critical book.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; questions of the book's obligation to German and to English writers, and the dates of its chapters, have been much studied, and the withdrawal of one chapter in later issues is documented in the author's own correspondence.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1817, in two volumes, by the author's regular publisher of those years, and reissued in the collected prose works later in the century; the several printings, the cancelled chapter and the borrowings charged against the author are recorded in the standard modern scholarly edition.

title: The Friend
description: A weekly literary and moral sheet conducted by the author at his own risk between 1809 and 1810, and reissued in an enlarged edition in 1812, in which the essayist addressed a small circle of subscribers on character, ambition, marriage, the duties of the young, the politics of the day and the principles of literature. It grew out of a scheme of public lectures on government and public feeling that had failed, and it carries that origin in its habit of arguing with an imaginary audience of men of business and of men of letters. The numbers mix moral meditation, literary criticism, autobiography and editorial matter, and the enterprise lost its projector money.
plot_or_argument: The essays proceed by proposition and appeal rather than by narrative: the writer states the condition of a private mind in a public age and then examines the resources available to it - habit, principle, the example of the ancients, the discipline of a chosen occupation. Some numbers deal with the conduct of life, warning against ambition without talent and against the love of reputation, and prescribing the economy of a character to be maintained in a world of parties; others comment on the literature and the criticism of the day, on the education of the mind and on the duties of the clergy, and on public affairs, including the conduct of the war and the state of the press. The whole is framed as a manual for a young man of character, and the series ends with the projector's plain account of the failure of the scheme, which became part of the biographical record of the author's life.
narrative_structure: A serial periodical of weekly numbers, gathered into a volume at the close of the first series and enlarged in the second edition of 1812; the numbers are free-standing, with a continuity of voice and of purpose rather than of argument, and with occasional letters and contributions from correspondents.
principal_characters: The essayist-editor addressing his subscribers; the imagined young man of character for whom the series is a manual; the friends and correspondents whose letters are inserted
literary_form: Periodical essay and moral-critical miscellany in the line of the Spectator papers, transformed by the Romantic habit of self-analysis and by the projector's account of his own enterprise.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of a dense and hortatory kind, marked by long sentences, abstract nouns and a repeated appeal to principle, with passages of narrative simplicity in the autobiographical numbers.
historical_context: Founded in London in 1809 after the failure of the author's lecture course on the state of public feeling and after the collapse of his domestic and marital prospects, at a time when the weekly literary sheet was being established as a vehicle for criticism and when the author's quarrel with his collaborator's public position was beginning; its financial failure left him dependent on lecture and periodical work for years.
