literary_significance: The chief monument of the author's own attempt to found a moral-literary journal, and a document of the Romantic essayist's quarrel with the market: its numbers on ambition, on the discipline of the mind and on the conduct of a public career are part of the period's preoccupation with character, and its material was later worked up in the literary autobiography of 1817.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; a few inserted letters and contributions by correspondents are distinguished from the projector's own matter in modern editions.
bibliographical_notes: Published weekly in London from 1809 to 1810, the numbers being put out by the author at his own charge, and reissued in an enlarged volume edition in 1812; the text, with its cancellations and the accounts of the scheme's failure, is edited in the modern collected prose works.

title: Aids to Reflection
description: The author's book of moral and religious reflection, published in 1825 and drawn from aphorisms, commentaries and letters on the conduct of the mind and the grounds of faith; the maxims and passages quoted from earlier writers, chiefly from a seventeenth-century divine, are set out with a running commentary that makes the book a work of applied philosophy rather than of devotion. Its purpose is to teach the reader to reflect, distinguishing the faculties by which he is governed and the order of knowledge proper to each, and its argument about reason and understanding became one of the most influential pieces of psychological vocabulary in the nineteenth century.
plot_or_argument: The work proceeds by aphorism and exposition. It divides the internal man into the powers of the flesh or appetite, the understanding with its prudence, and the reason with its moral and spiritual ideas, and argues that the errors of the age arise from applying the logic of the understanding to the objects of reason, so that prudence is mistaken for wisdom and the evidence of things seen for the evidence of things not seen. Against the philosophy of mere prudence it maintains that the moral will is the seat of personality and that the ideas of reason are not generalisations from experience but conditions of thought; the Christian faith is presented as a temper of heart requiring a readiness to be taught rather than a conclusion from proof. The closing letters and appendixes pursue the same distinction in disputes on free-will, on the character of the religious teacher, and on the temper of the church and its clergy, and it was these passages that drew the book into controversy with the author's own family and with the liberal religious bodies.
narrative_structure: A book of aphorisms with continuous commentary, arranged in several divisions and followed by letters and appendixes on the disputed questions; there is no narrative, and the design is that of an education of the reader's faculties, each division taking up one power of the mind.
literary_form: Moral and religious reflection in the aphoristic and commentarial manner, a work of practical philosophy written for the private reader and drawing on the seventeenth-century devotional writers as its quoted authorities.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of a deliberately weighty and periodic style, full of distinction and definition, with long sentences that enact the act of reflection and a repeated vocabulary of faculties, grounds and temper; it is the author's most quoted English prose.
historical_context: Published in 1825, in the years of the author's settlement as a household writer, of the controversies over the unitarian and Trinitarian questions, and of his public quarrels with the political and religious opinions of his early friends; the book's use of a seventeenth-century divine's maxims reflects the period's recovery of the older English theological writers.
literary_significance: One of the most widely read and most quoted books of Victorian thought, exercised through the distinction between reason and understanding and through its claim that religion is a temper of heart rather than a system of proof; readers from the schoolmaster and the cleric to the American transcendentalists formed their vocabulary of the faculties from it. It also remains the standard document of the religious turn of the later Romantic movement and of the author's own career.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the quoted aphorisms are the author's selection from an earlier divine and are acknowledged as such in the text.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1825, in a volume of the author's collected prose, and reissued in later editions with additions and with the letters on the controversies that followed its appearance; the selection of maxims, and the several revised issues, are recorded in the modern collected edition.

title: Joan of Arc
alternative_titles: Joan of Arc, an Epic Poem
description: An epic poem in twelve books on the Maid of Orleans, written in the first fervour of the author's republican enthusiasm and published in 1796 when he was barely over twenty, by subscription and through a Bristol printer, with a prefatory address that announced the plan of a national epic on a subject of Christian chivalry. It is a war epic and a poem of prophetic voices: the French shepherdess who hears the saints and leads an army, is rejected at the court and at the siege, and is finally taken and burnt, is the subject of a poem that gives its supernatural machinery a serious moral function.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens in the civil war of France and England and in the divinely warned dream of the maid, who is sent to relieve Orleans and to lead the Dauphin to his coronation. Books of council and of battle follow, in which the English commanders take counsel with dark powers and the maid's visions and prayers counter the machinery of her enemies; the field-worship of the French is raised above the war-craft of the invaders in a series of sieges, single combats and nights of watch, and the poem closes with the Maid taken at the last, condemned and committed to the fire, the epic ending in martyrdom rather than in triumph. The argument is at once patriotic and moral, making the virtue of an untaught peasant girl the measure of the kingdoms about her and the promise of deliverance the ground of her authority.
narrative_structure: An epic in twelve books with a continuous war narrative, framed by invocations, councils of gods and powers, prophetic dream and prophetic speech, and by long episodes of battle and siege; the machinery is distributed between the celestial guardians of the heroine and the dark advisers of her enemies.
principal_characters: Joan, the Maid of Orleans; the Dauphin, afterwards Charles the Seventh; the shepherds and the parents of the maid; the English commanders and their counsellors of the dark power; the saints who visit and encourage the heroine
literary_form: National epic in the heroic manner, on the model of the Christian epics of the older poems and of the war epic then being revived; its politics and its machinery mark it as a poem of the revolutionary decade.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, iambic pentameter, sustained through the twelve books with an unrhymed flow and occasional apostrophical excursions, in a style imitating the epics of the previous century rather than the polished diction of recent narrative verse.
historical_context: Composed during the author's undergraduate years at Oxford, in the first years of the French Revolution and of the English debating societies, and in the company of the communitarian scheme on the American frontier which occupied the same circle; its republican sympathy with France against England put it squarely in the radical poetry of the 1790s, from which the writer's later career was a long retreat.
literary_significance: The earliest ambitious English epic of the Romantic generation and the document of a radical young poet's attempt to found a national poem on the subject of a martyred maiden; its reputation rests mainly on its history and on the contrast between its politics and its author's later years, and its subject was a standing point of reference in the controversy over the epic in English.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1796 by subscription and printed at Bristol; the scheme's failure to obtain sufficient support is recorded in the author's later memoir of his own life. The poem was reprinted in the collected poetical works, where its revisions and the author's later annotations are documented.

title: Thalaba the Destroyer
description: An Oriental romance in verse, published in 1801 and described by its author as a tale of the East, in which a young man of the race of the destroyer of magic goes in quest of his betrothed through a desert peopled by genii, sorcerers and the relics of an old superstition. Its plan was to build an English poem on the machinery of Eastern romance and on the single providence of a faith without idols, and its experiments in a new prosody were among the most discussed versification projects of the decade.
plot_or_argument: Thalaba, son of the line whose office is to destroy the hosts of magic, is bound by a vow of chastity and obedience to a pilgrimage that shall lead him to the promised bride, and the poem follows his way through desert, cavern and enchanted city, with the powers of the old superstition pressing on him and the guardian spirit of his race failing at intervals to direct him. The beloved of the hero is preserved through captivity and rites of fire, and the episodes of the journey - the magicians, the sepulchres, the hollow music of the enchanted halls, the trials of thirst and the victories over the servants of the evil law - carry the poem's religion of trust in one invisible God. The argument ends with the destruction of the hosts of the sorcerers, the final abandonment of the guardian spirit, who is withheld from Thalaba at the last because the hero must learn to depend on Providence alone, and the accomplishment of the vow.
narrative_structure: A romantic quest in twelve books, organised as a string of episodes of trial and deliverance in a desert landscape, with the machinery of Eastern tale and a prophetic and guardian spirit whose intermittent absence is itself the poem's moral instrument.
principal_characters: Thalaba, the destroyer of magic; his betrothed and beloved; the guardian spirit of his ancestors; the sorcerers and the hosts of the evil law; the hermit and the companions of the desert
literary_form: Metrical tale and Oriental romance in verse, a philosophical tale of providence and temptation constructed on the machinery of Eastern narrative as then known to English readers.
meter_and_prosody: A deliberately experimental accentual prosody, in which the lines are measured by the number of accents rather than by syllables, and the stanzaic pattern is varied with the scene, sometimes in long flowing periods and sometimes in short and reiterated lines; the poet's own preface defended this treatment at length.
historical_context: Composed in the years of the author's retirement in the west and of his marriage, and published in 1801 with a preface on the principles of English prosody; its Eastern machinery drew on the translations of Arabian and Persian tales then current, and its monotheism was written as an answer to the idolatrous apparatus of the fashionable romance.
literary_significance: The boldest of the Romantic experiments in a new English prosody and the earliest serious English poem to take its machinery wholly from Eastern tale; the preface on accentual measurement is a document of the period's versification debates. Its reputation has declined, but it remains the standard instance of the quest poem built on providence rather than on chivalry.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1801, in two volumes, with a preface on prosody that was separately discussed in the reviews; revised in later editions of the author's poetical works, which carry the annotations on the Eastern machinery.

title: Madoc
alternative_titles: Madoc, a Welsh Poem
description: A long metrical romance on the Welsh legend of the twelfth-century prince who sailed westward and is reported to have reached and settled in America, published in 1805 after many years of revision. The poem joins the machinery and the civil war of medieval Wales to a voyage of discovery and a settlement in the western ocean, and its argument, openly stated in its closing invocation, is that the tale of a Welsh colony in America should serve as a bond of kindred between the two nations.
plot_or_argument: The young princes Madoc and his brother are estranged by a quarrel of succession and a crime that is charged on the one and denied; Madoc, sailing west with a small company in search of a new home, is driven by storms past the islands of the Atlantic to a coast of a green and abundant country, where he encounters nations of people at war one with another, their customs and their superstitions drawn at length. Madoc and his Welsh companies assist one nation against its enemies, the prince's skill in war and in council winning the good opinion of his new allies, and the settlement is at last secured by a marriage, while the brother's expedition across the ocean brings a like fate to a southern region and the two Welsh colonies are said to flourish apart from the Old World. The argument thus moves from civil war in Wales to the founding of an American commonwealth, and the poem closes by anticipating a time when the descendants of the colonies shall be one people with their parent nation.
narrative_structure: A metrical romance in twenty-two books, in two parallel histories - the Welsh expedition under the prince and the later voyage of his brother - with long episodes of council, battle, shipwreck and description of the American coast and its peoples; the two threads are brought together only in the closing argument of the poet.
principal_characters: Madoc, the Welsh prince; his brother, the rival claimant to the succession; their father, the aged king; the chiefs and warriors of the nations of the western coast; the companions and counsellors of the settlement
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, and a national or founding epic of the discoverer type, combining Welsh legend, the voyage narrative and the imaginary history of an American settlement.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse in a rapid and unelaborated movement, with occasional shorter stanzas for the songs and the lyrical interpolations; the versification was revised repeatedly, the earlier radical manner being smoothed in the printings of the nineteenth century.
historical_context: Begun in the years of the French Revolution and of the communitarian projects, when the author and his friends hoped for an asylum in the new world, and revised and at last published in 1805, in the decade of the transatlantic republic and of the renewed English interest in the discoverer legends; its plea of a Welsh blood-tie with America belongs to the poet's design of a literature serving an Atlantic kinship.
literary_significance: The most ambitious English romance of the Welsh-America legend and a document of the period's habit of inventing a genealogy for the New World out of the Celtic west; its subject was much imitated in later British and American verse and its claim of a shared descent is a standing instance of Romantic transatlantic imagining.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Begun in the 1790s and repeatedly revised; first published London, 1805, in two volumes, and reprinted in the collected poetical works, where the changes made between the manuscript and the printed text are recorded.

title: The Curse of Kehama
alternative_titles: Kehama
description: An Oriental tale in verse published in 1810, founded on the machinery of the Hindu theology as it was then known in translation, and telling of a sacrilegious Brahmin who dares the powers of heaven and is pursued by a curse. The poem's design was to make an English epic out of an Eastern religion, giving its subordinate spirits, its places of punishment and its hierarchy of gods a continuous narrative function, and its argument is that the defier of the moral order is destroyed while the innocent suffer briefly for his guilt.
plot_or_argument: Kehama, a Brahmin of boundless ambition, obtains by violence the bride of another man and, having set at defiance the powers that govern the world of spirits, is struck by the curse pronounced upon him, which pursues him through the books of the poem. The machinery works continuously: inferior ministers of the divine justice are sent to execute the sentence, and the guilty man's prosperity is made to turn to the ruin of those about him, while a patient and devoted member of his own house, whose life is spent in endurance and devotion, is taken out of suffering rather than preserved to enjoy it. The last books bring the curse to its execution, the destroyer of Kehama's happiness being himself destroyed, and the poem ends with the justification of the moral government of the universe and with the assurance that the obedient and the meek are remembered by the powers they serve.
narrative_structure: A metrical tale in a long series of books, organised as the pursuit of one guilty man by a supernatural sentence, with the action of the machinery intermixed with the domestic calamities of the mortals; the argument is carried by episodes of temptation, punishment and patience rather than by a continuous plot.
principal_characters: Kehama, the sacrilegious Brahmin; the bride carried off by his violence and her kindred; the ministers and subordinate spirits of the Hindu theology who execute the curse; a patient and devoted member of the offender's own house
literary_form: Metrical tale and romance in verse, and an Oriental philosophical poem of the providential type, in which the machinery of a living religion is used as the apparatus of a moral fable.
meter_and_prosody: An accentual versification of the experimental kind already tried in the author's earlier Eastern tale, with lines measured by stress rather than by syllable count and a stanza that varies with the scene, the whole giving a rolling and reiterated effect much remarked on by the reviewers.
historical_context: Published in 1810, when translations of Hindu scripture and commentary were supplying English poets with a new apparatus of machinery, and when the author had settled into the Lake community and was moving from the radicalism of the 1790s towards the conservative religious position of his later years; the poem's theodicy belongs to that transition.
literary_significance: The most elaborate of the Romantic English poems built wholly on Hindu machinery, and a document of the period's appetite for an epic apparatus drawn from the religions of the East; its treatment of the curse as an engine of narrative influenced later Oriental tale in verse, and its theology of patience and punishment is a plain instance of the religious temper of the author's middle years.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1810, in a single volume with an argument and notes explaining the machinery; revised in the collected poetical works, where the author's later annotations on his sources in the Oriental scholarship of the day are recorded.

title: Wat Tyler
alternative_titles: Wat Tyler: A Dramatic Poem
description: A dramatic poem on the rising of 1381, written in the summer of 1794 in the heat of the author's republican enthusiasm and kept from print until 1817, when it was issued with two other plays. It is a political closet drama in which the peasants of Kent and Essex, provoked by the poll-tax and by the cruelty of the tax-gatherers, march on London under the leader whose name gives the poem its title, and where the demands of the rebels are argued at length by a preaching priest of the insurrection. Its publication in 1817, in a season of domestic repression, gave offence and brought the printer into trouble for the politics it contained.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins with the insult offered to a peasant's daughter by an officer of the excise and with the summary killing that lights the country fire; the rustics of Kent and Essex gather, choose their leader, and are heartened by the itinerant preacher who argues that all men were born free and that the bondage of the poor is the work of the covetous and of their laws. The rebels come to London, are received with promises by the young king, and obtain a charter, after which the leader is treacherously summoned to a conference, struck down before the lord mayor and beheaded, the insurrection ending in the revoked promises and in the executed peasant. The argument is an open plea for the rights of the oppressed, in which the dialogue of the commons, the priest and the leader states the case for resistance and the closing scene states the price of defeat.
narrative_structure: A dramatic poem in several acts, written for the reader rather than for the stage, moving from the single provoking insult to the mustering of the counties, the march and the parley with the king, and the betrayal and execution; the political case is carried in set speeches and in the debate between the preacher and the peasant leader.
principal_characters: Wat Tyler, the leader of the commons; the itinerant priest who preaches the equality of mankind; the chiefs of the Kentish and Essex rebels; King Richard the Second and his council; the officers of the tax and the lord mayor of London
literary_form: Closet drama and dramatic poem on a popular rising, in the line of the republican historical plays of the revolutionary decade, with the choruses and the debates of the commons taking the place of the stage machinery.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of a plain and declamatory kind, with short speech-lines and a share of rhymed and song-like passage for the commons, deliberately free of the polish of the fashionable drama of the 1790s.
historical_context: Composed in 1794, the year of the repression of the English radical societies, of the Treason trials and of the author's own communitarian hopes, in company with a friend and fellow-planter of the same schemes; withheld from press for more than twenty years, it appeared in 1817 amid the prosecutions for libel and sedition that followed the peace, and its publication was used against the author's politics in the reviews of the later 1820s and 1830s.
literary_significance: The most direct English drama of the 1790s to make a medieval peasant rising the figure of contemporary revolutionary argument, and one of the documents by which the later reputation of the Lake school was contested: its appearance in print long after composition forced readers to reconsider the relation between the radical writings of the period and the conservatism of their authors. It remains a standard text for the literature of the poll-tax rising and for the Romantic drama of revolt.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the circumstances of its joint composition and its long suppression are documented in the author's correspondence and in the memoir written by his successor.
bibliographical_notes: Written 1794; first published London, 1817, in a volume with two other dramatic poems, the issue of the volume leading to a prosecution of the publisher for its politics; the text was not reprinted in the author's lifetime, and the history of the suppression and of the 1817 volume is recorded in the collected editions.

title: The Life of Nelson
alternative_titles: The Life of Horatio, Viscount Nelson
description: A short prose biography of Admiral Viscount Nelson, published within months of the subject's death at Trafalgar and written by the poet who had spent the years of the Peninsular War in Portugal and had collected materials there. It was planned as one life in a series of the worthies of the country, and it rapidly became the standard account, passing through many editions and giving the national story of Nelson its permanent shape.
plot_or_argument: The life follows the admiral from his entry as a boy into the service and his apprenticeship in the Arctic and the East Indies, through the losses of his right eye and his right arm, to the Mediterranean command, the battle of the Nile, and the Neapolitan episode, and then to the blockade of Toulon, the pursuit of the enemy fleet across the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, and the battle of Trafalgar, in which he was killed at the moment of victory. The narrative is built on the letters and the journals of the subject, quoted at length, and on the documents of the actions described, and it draws from them a portrait of a commander whose prudence, care for his officers and sailors, and religious faith were as remarkable as his daring. The argument is that a rector's son of Norfolk had made himself the instrument of his country's safety by steady attention, humanity and courage, and that his greatest victories were won before the action that killed him.
narrative_structure: A continuous prose life in a single volume, chronological and documentary, with the subject's own letters and the official papers of the actions interwoven, and with brief reflective passages on the character and on the use of biography; there is no dramatic partition of the matter.
principal_characters: Horatio Viscount Nelson; his father, the rector of Burnham Thorpe, and the kindred of his boyhood; his officers and the seamen of his fleet; the adversaries whom he encountered at the Nile and at Trafalgar
literary_form: Prose biography of the short national type, combining the memoir built on letters with the account of campaigns, and written for a general reader rather than for the navy.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of unusual clearness and compression, in plain periods of narrative and quotation, with a habit of pointed summary at the end of the action; the book is commonly cited as a model of English biographical prose.
historical_context: Written in 1813, in the middle of the Peninsular War and after the author's residence in Portugal as secretary to the commander-in-chief, when the nation's need of a hero after the death of Nelson and the fame of Trafalgar made the subject a public claim; the life was part of a plan of national biography and appeared in the same years as the author's appointment to the laurelship.
literary_significance: The most durable English biography of Nelson and one of the most reprinted prose works of the period, fixed in the schools and in the gift-book trade of the nineteenth century as the account of the admiral; it is also the document that showed the Lake poet's later career at its most effective, and its method of building a life out of quoted letters was much imitated.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1813, in a single volume, and reprinted in many editions, the author revising the text for a later issue; the Portuguese journals and letters gathered in the Peninsula are the basis of the work, and the several editions are recorded in the collected prose works.

title: Songs of Innocence
alternative_titles: Songs of Innocence. Written for the Children of the Age to Come
description: A short collection of lyrics etched, printed and hand-coloured by the author himself in 1789, and issued as plates with the poems and the designs engraved on the same copper, so that text and image were made as one object. Its voices are those of children, of the piper who is taught by them, of the lamb, the nurse, the chimney-sweeper and the schoolboy, and its subject is a state of the human soul in which protection, joy and trust are still unbroken. It was later combined with a second collection to show the two contrary states of the human soul.
plot_or_argument: The poems present a world of open country and of the city's poor in which innocence is both a fact and a condition exposed to danger. A piper hears a child asking for a song about a lamb, writes it, and rejoices; another song answers the child's question about who made the lamb by tracing the maker's meek and gentle likeness in himself. The lamb, the little black boy, the chimney-sweepers of London, the nurse whose play is over, the schoolboy who watches the winter morning and the evening's returning flock, and the shepherd and the boy who has lost his ball, give a sequence of small states of the soul; two of the poems name the cruelty of the institutions that employ children and one of them sets the child's complaint against the prayer and the doctrine taught him, so that the collection's innocence is figured as a trust that others are ready to betray. The closing poems turn to the grown-ups who have lost that trust, and the little bird, the clod and the pebble give the short lyric argument about the answerable heart.
narrative_structure: A plate-for-plate collection of short lyrics, without a continuous story but designed as a sequence, the order of the illuminated copies varying slightly and the images supplying a running commentary on the texts; the poems answer one another by their repeated figures of the child, the maker and the guardian.
principal_characters: The child who asks the piper to write a song; the lamb and its questioning child; the little black boy; the chimney-sweepers Tom Dacre and his fellow workers; the nurse and the schoolboy; the shepherd, the blossoms and the lost boy; the piper who becomes the writer of the songs
literary_form: Illuminated lyric collection and songs of the innocent state, in the line of the nursery song and the devotional hymn, engraved and designed by the poet as a single art object.
meter_and_prosody: Short song stanzas of two- and three-beat lines with simple recurring rhyme, many of them written as airs to be sung, with repetitions and question-and-answer patterns proper to children's verse; the irregularities are part of the song manner rather than errors of the ear.
historical_context: Etched and printed in London in 1789, when the author had developed his method of illuminated relief-printing and was working as an engraver and designer of plates in the City; its concern with children, with the sweeper chimneys of the metropolis and with the teachings of the church belongs to the philanthropic and dissenting writing of that decade.
literary_significance: The founding work of the illuminated books and one of the two collections that make up the standard Romantic statement of innocence and experience as contrary states; its songs entered the anthologies of children's verse and its plates are the central example of the poet's method of making text and design one. Its account of protected and betrayed childhood remains a starting point of modern criticism of the lyric of innocence.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the several hand-coloured copies differ in the order of the plates and in the colouring, and the number of copies printed from the copper plates is a matter of bibliography rather than of disputed authorship.
bibliographical_notes: Etched, printed and coloured by the author in London in 1789 as a set of plates, the title plate naming the collection and describing it as written for the children of the future age; re-issued in 1794 combined with the second collection under a single title describing the two contrary states of the soul. Surviving hand-coloured copies vary in the order of the plates, and the modern facsimile editions reproduce the several states of the copper.

title: Songs of Experience
description: The second and darker of the two illuminated collections, etched and printed by the author in 1794 and issued with the earlier songs under a single title announcing the two contrary states of the human soul. Its lyrics answer, correct and destroy the trust of the first collection: the maker of the lamb is now questioned as the maker also of the tiger, the garden of innocence is planted with a chapel, and the poems of the city expose the institutions, the priests and the kings that keep the soul in bondage.
plot_or_argument: The collection opens with an earth answerable to the eternal, and with the tiger, whose frightful symmetry forces the question of what hand or eye could frame such dread and what exchange of fear was made when it was given life, an answer that reverses the child's trust in the lamb. Songs of the lost childhood follow: the sick rose destroyed by the invisible worm, the sunflower pined out in the marsh, the grey-bearded physician who knows the tree by its leaf and nothing else, and the youth who is told that the garden of love, where his infant joys were planted, is now a chapel, its gates shut against the child and its altar dressed with the thorns and briars of the priest's curse. The later plates turn on London and on the moral state of the kingdom, in which every black'ning church, the palace rebuilt from the blood of the soldier, the marriage hearse and the cries of the chimney-boy are read as a state of bondage, and the poems of the harlot, of the flies of summer and of the little lost one close upon pity for the sinner and the child, so that the contrary state is presented at once as knowledge and as the loss of the power to feel. The last poem figures the bard of a new age who shall restore the departed powers.
narrative_structure: A plate-for-plate collection answering the earlier songs poem by poem, with a progression from the tiger and the lost garden through the city poems to the harlot and the closing promise of the bard; several pieces exist in two versions in the earlier copy, and the design of the sequence is the collection's argument.
principal_characters: The tiger and the questioning singer; the rose and the invisible worm; the sun-flower and the lily of the valley; the grey-bearded sage; the child who sees the chapel in the garden of love; the harlot of the city of London; the soldier, the chimney-sweeper and the labouring poor of the London plates; the little lost one; the bard of the new age
literary_form: Illuminated lyric collection and songs of the experienced state, in the line of the song and the emblem, designed as a direct reply to the earlier collection and printed with its plates as one book.
meter_and_prosody: Song stanzas of two- and three-beat lines with a tightened and more reiterated pattern, the tiger's trochaic four-beat lines and its insistent questions being the most quoted example; the rhythm is deliberately hammer-like where the argument demands it, and the later plates allow longer and more prophetic periods.
historical_context: Etched and printed in London in 1794, in the years of the author's most active experiment with illuminated relief-printing and in the decade of the repression of English radical opinion, the wars with France and the trade in wealth of the metropolis, all of which give the city poems their targets; the combined issue of the two collections under one title states the theory of contrary states from which the poems proceed.
literary_significance: One of the two collections that define the Romantic reading of innocence and experience as contrary and answering states of the soul, and the source of the most discussed single lyric in English on the problem of the maker of evil. Its plates are the standard evidence of the poet's illuminated method, and its London poems are a permanent part of the literature of the city and of the critique of institutional religion.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the existence of earlier drafts of several poems, and the differences between the copies in the order of the plates, are matters of bibliography and of the text's several states.
bibliographical_notes: Etched, printed and coloured by the author in London in 1794 and issued combined with the earlier collection under a single title-plate describing the two contrary states of the human soul; surviving copies differ in the order of the plates and in the colouring, and the modern facsimile and scholarly editions print the several states.

title: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
alternative_titles: Marriage of Heaven and Hell
description: The most argumentative of the illuminated books, etched and printed by the author in the years following the two collections of songs, and written in a mixed prose and verse manner after the model of a prophetic book and in open parody of the religious tables then current. Its occasion is a memory of a hell where the spirits of the dead are taught by an angel, and its case is that without contraries there is no progression, and that the energies called devilish are the active and creative half of the human soul, while the heaven of patient receiving and the morality of the priesthood are its passive and repressive half.
plot_or_argument: The book opens with the proposition that without contraries there is no progression, and that attraction and repulsion, energy and reason, are necessary to existence, and then reports a memorable fancy in which the author sees in hell an angel sleeping, wakes him, and finds that the angel's religion of patience and of the outward law is undone by the teaching of the place. The voice of the devil follows, arguing that worship is the blessing of the strong to the weak, that the gospel's teacher was a philanthropist and not a priest, and that the true religion is the delight of the senses and the energies of desire. A series of proverbs of Hell then states in short sentences a counter-morality of excess, of the desire that is not executed, of the tigers of wrath being wiser than the horses of instruction, and of the prison and the brothel as built with the stones of law and the bricks of religion. The middle plates give the lights of the six senses, the types of moral character, and a passage on the sacred books of the East, and the book closes with a song of liberty, in which the dragon of the old state is kindled and overthrown and the voices of the morning cry aloud among the nations of the west.
narrative_structure: A continuous illuminated argument in plates, mixing vision, oration, proverb, catalogue and closing song; the parts are bound by the claim that the book's teaching is the doctrine of contraries, and by the figure of the narrator who reports what the spirits of hell said to him.
principal_characters: The narrator who records the dream of the sleeping angel; the angel of the book's vision; the voice of the devil, who dictates the book's creed; the daughters of memory and the phantoms of the closed song of liberty
literary_form: Illuminated prophetic book and verse-and-prose satire, partly a parody of the devotional table and of the prophetic writing then current, and partly a manifesto of the contrary energies of the soul.
meter_and_prosody: Chiefly prose of a rapid, gnomic and declamatory kind, with the proverbs in balanced and pointed sentences and the verse passages in short reiterated song lines, the whole varying between the sermon, the aphorism and the air.
historical_context: Etched and printed in London in the years immediately after the two collections of songs, in the decade of the English reception of the new religious writings from the Continent and of the controversy about the French Revolution; the book's attack on the priesthood, on the law and on a religion of patience is written out of the radical religious argument of the 1790s.
literary_significance: The founding text of the poet's own prophetic system and the most widely read of his illuminated books, the source of his most quoted sentences on contraries, on the energies of desire and on the institutions built by the law, and the standing example of the Romantic prose-verse pamphlet. Its closing song of liberty made it a permanent document of revolutionary writing, and its argument supplied the terms in which later readers described the imagination's enmity to the moral system.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date of the first issue is fixed by the internal evidence of the plates and by the author's later references rather than by a printed title page.
bibliographical_notes: Etched and printed by the author in London, generally assigned to the years about 1790 to 1793, in an illuminated issue of which the surviving copies differ in the order of the plates; it was reprinted in the collected works of the nineteenth century and has been facsimiled and separately edited several times.

title: Visions of the Daughters of Albion
description: An illuminated verse tract etched and printed by the author in 1793, written as a vision addressed to the daughters of a benighted island, and built on a single situation of violated love and disputed possession. A planter of the western colonies takes a bound girl by force while her lover, a pale youth of speculative sorrow, does nothing to save her, and the poem argues from that situation that desire denied, jealousy brooding in the mind, and the law of another's property in a human body are all one tyranny.
plot_or_argument: The poem is framed as an address to the daughters of Albion, who sit in a rockbound shore and are bidden to awake and see what the senses of the Slaves of America have endured. Oothoon, the bound girl, goes to the grove with her flowers and is taken by Bromion, the thunder-footed planter of the West Indies, who brands her as his possession and boasts of the rape to Theotormon, the jealous and contemplative youth who loved her. Oothoon pleads that her soul is free and that no clod of a body can bind the daughter of the morning, and she calls on the slaves of the east and the west to rise; Theotormon, unable to answer her, sits in the cave and questions the winds, the beasts and the star of the morning, tortured by a jealousy he cannot name and by a religion that forbids him to pity. The poem closes with the awakening of the daughters and the declaration that where there is no desire there is no virtue, and that the state of the slave and the state of the inhibited lover are one state.
narrative_structure: A visionary tract in long blank-verse lines, framed as an address to a chorus of daughters and organised as a single situation reported in three voices, with the pleading of the injured girl, the boasts of the planter and the questioning solitude of the lover alternating; the poem's argument is carried by the speeches rather than by incident.
principal_characters: Oothoon, the bound girl of the plantations; Bromion, the thunder-footed planter of the West Indies; Theotormon, her lover, a youth of jealous speculation; the daughters of Albion, addressed as a chorus; the slaves of the east and the west invoked in her plea
literary_form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, a tract of liberty written in the manner of the prophetic book and drawing its situation from the contemporary controversy over slavery and over the rights of desire.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of an irregular and vehement kind, with long overrunning periods, apostrophes and reiterated questions, and a few short lyrical interpolations; the lines vary in beat and are printed as part of the illuminated design.
historical_context: Etched and published in London in 1793, the year of the controversy over the slave trade and of the poet's most active sympathy with the revolutions of France and America; its plea for the slave and its attack on a law that makes a body property belong to the radical religious writing of that decade, and its title names the island whose daughters are asleep.
literary_significance: The most sustained Romantic poem on the identity of sexual and civil bondage, and one of the earliest English works to make the enslaved woman's own speech the vehicle of an argument for liberty; it is central to modern readings of the poet's myth of desire and jealousy, and its situation has been a standing example in the criticism of abolitionist and feminist reading of the 1790s.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Etched, printed and coloured by the author in London in 1793 as one of the illuminated books, the copies differing in the order and colouring of the plates; reprinted in the collected works of the nineteenth century and separately edited in the modern facsimile and scholarly series.

title: America a Prophecy
alternative_titles: America: A Prophecy
description: An illuminated prophecy etched and printed in 1793, written as a vision of the American war of independence seen as an act of spiritual liberation, and addressed in its preface to the inhabitants of a great republic. Its machinery centres on a youth born of a woman's terror on the night when the king's son was slain, who becomes the fire of revolt, and on the watchful angel and the dark power of the deep who would hold the old world in its chains; the poem makes the Atlantic revolution the opening of a new age for the nations of the west.
plot_or_argument: The preface, addressed to the people of the newly founded republic, declares that the moment is come when the oppressor shall fall, and that the blood of the victims cries from the ground. In the vision that follows, the Angel of England, watchful on the rock of the hoary king, is driven from his sleep, and the spectre of the old king calls on the dark spirit of the deep to arm; meanwhile the youth Orc, born in a night of terror when his mother saw the king's son slain by the sinner who was also the avenger, grows up in the wild and is fed by the vultures of the morning, and at sixteen is drawn to the burning fires of revolution. Orc, joined by the female spirit of the west who weeps over him and is bound in chains of the sun's rays, breaks the doors of the dungeon where the hoary black Angel keeps his books, and with him the multitude of the oppressed, driven mad with the expectation of a coming day, pass across the ocean; the poem ends with the fall of the cities of the west and with the voice of the liberated land, the nations of the ocean and the children of the new age crying aloud at the opening of the morning.
narrative_structure: A prophecy in two parts, a prose preface and a blank-verse vision, organised as the birth and the action of a spirit of revolt, with the machinery of angels, kings' spirits and chained female powers; the argument moves from the watchful angel over the rock to the breaking of the dungeon and the passage of the oppressed to the new world.
principal_characters: Orc, the youth who is the spirit of revolt; his mother, the terrified woman of the vision; the Angel of England, hoary and watching on the rock; the dark power of the deep; the female spirit of the west, bound in chains; the multitude of the oppressed and the inhabitants of the new republic
literary_form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, a political prophecy that casts the American Revolution as the first act of a spiritual emancipation.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of a rapid and reiterating kind, with long breathless periods, apostrophe and the short shouted lines of the closing chorus; the preface is in prose of an oracle-like brevity.
historical_context: Etched and published in London in 1793, in the year of the war with France, of the trial of the author's fellow-citizen for his Corresponding Society, and of the height of the English debate about the American and French revolutions; the poem's dedication to the inhabitants of a great republic and its figure of the oppressor's fall belong to that moment of revolutionary hope.
literary_significance: The boldest of the poet's revolutionary prophecies and the standard instance of his identification of political insurrection with imaginative liberation; its figure of the youth Orc, born in terror and bred in rebellion, became the central recurring personage of his later myth. It is a permanent document of the literature of the Atlantic revolutions and of the claim that a new nation might be the subject of a new prophecy.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Etched, printed and coloured by the author in London in 1793 as one of the illuminated books, the preface naming the inhabitants of the great republic as its audience; later copies differ in the order of the plates, and the book was reprinted in the collected works and edited separately in the modern series.

title: Europe a Prophecy
alternative_titles: Europe: A Prophecy
description: The second of the illuminated prophecies of the revolutionary decade, etched and printed in 1794 and written as a vision of Europe sunk in a long night of kings, priests and built walls, from which a spirit of revolt at last breaks forth. The American act of the preceding prophecy is here followed by the European reaction, and the poem's argument is that the old continent, watched by its cyclops builders and its grey priests, is delivered not by counsel but by the fires of a new imagination.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the night of the fallen church and of the kings of Europe, and with the sleep of Albion's daughters; the powers of the dead king's mother, the grey priest and the builders of the golden walls, who measure and fortify the continent against the voice of the people, hold the hour of darkness. A female power, bound and weeping, is watched over by the cycle of years, and the grey daughters of the old state are summoned to the sound of a trumpet. The central action is the coming of the youth of fire, who, urged by the female spirit of the west, descends upon the cities of Europe, and the closing plates give the fall of the built and measured order, the breaking of the seals of the grey books, and the voice of the awakened earth, the poem ending with the announcement that the hour is accomplished and that the morning is come for the nations of the old world.
narrative_structure: A prophecy in two movements, a long night-piece of the sleeping and fortified continent and a short catastrophe of fire and trumpet, with an elaborate machinery of kings, priests, builders and bound female powers; the verse carries the argument by vision and proclamation rather than by incident.
principal_characters: The grey priest and the builders of the golden walls; the female powers of the old continent, watchful and bound; the youth of fire who descends upon Europe; the spirit of the west; the grey daughters of the old state, summoned to the trumpet
literary_form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, a political vision of the European reaction following the American revolution, written in the same prophetic manner as its predecessor.
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of solemn and reiterated movement, with short chorus-lines and the flourish of the closing proclamation; the poet's own note on the verse, added when the book was reissued, explains the design of the lines.
historical_context: Etched and published in London in 1794, in the year of the Terror, of the war and of the repression of the English societies, and of the author's own most openly revolutionary printing; the poem's picture of a continent walled by priests and builders is a comment on the reaction that had overtaken the hopes of the previous five years.
literary_significance: The completest statement of the poet's early revolutionary myth and, with its companion prophecy, the foundation of his later system of the four continents and their binding powers; its images of the measured and fortressed Europe are a permanent part of Romantic writing about the old order, and the book's argument that imagination rather than reform delivers the nations shaped all his later work.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the dating of the issue and the relation of the several copies' plate order are matters of bibliography rather than of authorship.
bibliographical_notes: Etched, printed and coloured by the author in London in 1794 as one of the illuminated books, with the date given on the title plate; it was reissued in later years with alterations and was reprinted in the collected works of the nineteenth century and edited separately in the modern facsimile series.

title: The Book of Urizen
alternative_titles: Urizen
description: The first of the great illuminated books of the poet's own myth, etched and printed in 1794 as a cosmogony in nine chapters, giving an account of the creation of the world as a fall. An eternal being of separate reason, who divides himself from the other powers and sets up a law of one, is the maker of a contracted and legal universe; his books, written in the dark proportions of his own solitude, are the law and the religion that bind mankind, and the poem tells of his revolt, his loss of a companion power, and the long age of priesthood and sacrifice that follows.
plot_or_argument: The first chapters describe the self-separation of the fourth power, who becomes a king and a lawgiver in a vacuum, calls his book and his priests into being, and sets the measure of a world in which all things are bounded and weighed. His companion joy, who is cast down from his side in the contest with the other powers, is lost to him, and the birth of the female powers and of the world of nature follows his fall, the creation being an act of division and of grief. In the middle chapters the new created world is given its seasons, its cities and its religions, and the priests of the law of one preach sacrifice and fear; the later chapters bring the revolt of the serpent and of the woman in the garden of the new-created race, the flood of sorrow, and the long dark age of the book and the law, closing with a vision of the day of judgment in which the fabricated universe is shaken and the powers of the dead are broken.
narrative_structure: A cosmogonic book in nine numbered chapters, proceeding by proclamation and narrative from the prime separation through the making of the bounded world to the age of law and the threatened dissolution; its design answers and parodies the book of Genesis, and the argument is carried in the fall and reign of a single reason-god.
principal_characters: Urizen, the fourth power who becomes king and lawgiver; his lost companion joy, called Ahania; the other eternal powers who contend with him; the priests and the books of the new law; the created female powers and the new-made race of the bounded world
literary_form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, a book of cosmogony and theodicy written as a scripture of the poet's own invention, with the chapter divisions and the style of a biblical book.
meter_and_prosody: Short and stern accentual lines of varying beat, mostly in common and ballad measures, with an insistent repetition of words and a harsh monosyllabic music appropriate to its law and its terrors; the several chapters vary their stanzaic pattern.
historical_context: Etched and published in London in 1794, in the year in which the poet issued the two books of songs and the European prophecy, and when his myth of a fallen reason was being formed out of his reading of the religious and philosophical systems of the day; its parody of a book of Moses and its attack on a religion of law belong to the same moment of revolutionary dissent.
literary_significance: The foundation of the poet's private prophecy and one of the most ambitious inventions of English Romantic verse: a creation myth in which reason, law and priesthood make a world of contraction, and in which the universe of single authority is presented as a fall from unity. Its Urizen has become a standard name in literary culture for the reasoning power set against imagination, and the book is central to all accounts of the Romantic myth-making.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the several issues of the book and the plates' arrangement in the surviving copies differ, and the myth's relations to the poet's other books are a matter of interpretation, not of authorship.
bibliographical_notes: Etched, printed and coloured by the author in London in 1794 as one of the illuminated books, with the date on the title plate; it was reissued in later years, and the surviving copies, which vary in plate order and colour, are described in the facsimile and scholarly editions.

title: Jerusalem
alternative_titles: Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion
description: The last and largest of the illuminated books, begun in the year of the poet's settlement at Felpham and completed in plates over many years of work, which gathers the whole of his earlier myth into a single vision of the awakening of a giant and the rebuilding of a city in England. It is written in two kinds of verse, a measured line for the narrative of Albion and a long blazing line for the prophecies, and it opens with a prose preface that states the poet's duty to build a system of his own rather than to be governed by another's.
plot_or_argument: The prose preface declares the poet's cause as vision and the defence of imagination against the men of single reason, and ends by invoking a new Jerusalem to be built in England's green and pleasant land among those dark satanic mills. The poem then tells how Albion, the ancient giant of all mankind, lies fallen and divided into the four Zoas or states of the soul, and how, in the night of his sleep, his emanation and the powers of loss and of error hold him in chains; the books trace the labours of the prophetic and creative power who works in the furnaces of the world to bring him back to unity. The argument passes through the histories of the daughters of Albion, of the priests of the law of one, and of the cities built in the name of measurement, and closes with the awakening of Albion, the reconciliation of the divided powers, and the vision of the Emanation gathered to the Man, the last plates declaring that the hour is come and that all the nations shall see the mercy of the Divine Humanity.
narrative_structure: A great illuminated book of over a hundred plates, divided into its own internal books and chapters, mixing narrative prophecy, song and dramatic dialogue, with the two metres and the two orders of argument alternating; the design is a single movement from the sleep of Albion to his awakening.
principal_characters: Albion, the ancient giant of all mankind; Los, the prophetic and creative power who labour in the furnaces; Enitharmon, his emanation; the four states or Zoas into which Albion is divided; Rahab and the powers of loss; the priests of the law of one and the builders of the cities of measurement
literary_form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, the sum of the poet's myth, and a national prophecy in the form of a scripture of the imagination.
meter_and_prosody: Two metres are used throughout: a measured and stately accentual line for the narrative and songs, and a long, reiterated and vehement line for the prophetic books, the verses being printed as part of the illuminated plates; the opening lyric and the closing hymn-like lines are among the most set to music in English.
historical_context: Begun at Felpham in Sussex in 1804, in the years of the poet's quarrel with his patron and of his return to London, and worked at in plates until the last decade of his life, when copies were issued by himself and by his wife; its imagery of the fallen giant and of the dark mills answers the industrial and national condition of England during and after the long war with France.
literary_significance: The most ambitious illuminated book and the final shape of the poet's prophetic system, and, through the lyric placed in its preface, the source of a poem that became one of the most sung of all English verses. Its claim that a city of imagination is to be built in the midst of a labouring nation is a permanent text both of Romantic theory and of later writing about England.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the date of completion and of the several issues of the plates, and the order in which the parts were executed, are matters of scholarship rather than of authorship.
bibliographical_notes: Begun in 1804 and executed in illuminated plates over many years, the copies being printed and sold by the author himself, with a printed title supplied for the completed set; the several copies, with their differences of plate order and colouring, are described in the facsimile editions, and the whole book is available in the standard scholarly reprint.

title: Essays of Elia
alternative_titles: The First Series of the Essays of Elia
description: A volume of familiar essays collected in 1823 from papers contributed to a London magazine over the preceding years under an assumed name, and comprising some of the most loved prose of the century. The persona of the essays is a gentle, retired, half-humble town writer who remembers his childhood, his brothers and sisters, the offices in which he worked, the plays and the books he has read, and the poor and the odd characters of the metropolis. Its manner is allusive, digressive and affectionate, and its best pieces, among them the reverie of the dream children and the dissertation upon roast pig, have never been out of print.
plot_or_argument: The essays have no plot but a succession of meditations and portraits. Some turn on the writer's own life: the counting-house and the India Office with their clerks, their pensioners and their usages, the decayed relations and the old country house, the reverie in which two children, invented as his own, are found to be the children of another, and the remembrance of the sister from whom a long and painful interval separates him. Others take up a class or a custom - the stage and the players of the old theatres, the chimney-sweepers and the beggars of the holiday streets, the roast pig of China and its inventors, the punsters and the poor relations, the actors of the great and little towns. A third group are studies of books and characters: the old drama and its heroes, a distant cousin of the family, and the meditations on the mercy of the rich and on the use of riches. The argument throughout is that the imaginative and tender reading of common life, in an age of hurry and of money-getting, is the truest wisdom available to a private man.
narrative_structure: A collection of free-standing essays, with no continuous scheme, arranged in an order that alternates the autobiographical, the character-sketch and the literary-critical pieces; the unity is that of the persona, whose memory and temperament connect all the subjects.
principal_characters: Elia, the retired and imaginative essayist; his sister; the children of the dream reverie; the clerks and pensioners of the counting-houses; the old actors and the odd characters of the London streets
literary_form: Familiar essay and character sketch in the revived line of the Elizabethan and of the eighteenth-century paper, written with the deliberate archaism and the personal digression that distinguish the Romantic essay from the Spectator manner.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of extraordinary flexibility, mixing the short sentence of gossip with the long periodic sentence charged with half-remembered quotation, the rhythm of the older English writers being imitated and transformed; the style is the essay's chief instrument of feeling.
historical_context: Written during the years in which the essayist, a London clerk by profession, contributed to the magazines of the day, and collected in 1823; the papers belong to the flourishing of the familiar essay in the 1820s and to the revival of interest in the old drama and its actors, and they are written out of a family history that included the calamity of 1796, in which his mother was killed and the surviving sister became the partner of his whole after-life.
literary_significance: The volume that defined the English familiar essay of the nineteenth century and made its persona a model for later writers of the personal paper; its pieces on the old plays, on the children of the dream and on the beggars of the metropolis are standard texts of the prose anthologies. It also fixed the writer's reputation as the chief link between the Elizabethan essayists and the prose of the Victorian period.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the essays were written under an assumed name, and a small number of magazine contributions of these years, printed elsewhere under other heads, are distinguished from the Elia papers in the collected editions.
bibliographical_notes: First collected London, 1823, the papers having appeared in a London magazine from 1820 onwards, some of them having been contributed earlier to other periodicals; a second series, entitled Last Essays, followed in 1833, and the magazine originals and the several printings are recorded in the modern collected edition.

title: The Last Essays of Elia
alternative_titles: Last Essays of Elia
Eliana
description: The second and last series of the familiar essays, gathered from the periodicals of the later 1820s and published in 1833, with an introductory letter affecting to come from a kinsman of the earlier persona. The voice is the same retired, book-loving and affectionate essayist of the first series, but the pieces are more various and sometimes more occasional, taking in the country, the universities, the pleasures of a day's excursion, and the quarrels and kindnesses of literary society. It contains some of the best of the later papers and the last of the essays written under the assumed name.
plot_or_argument: The volume moves between reminiscence, portrait and travel. Several papers revisit the first series' country of childhood and of relationship, and one of them returns to the sister and to the old houses of the family history with a gravity the earlier essays had held in check. Others are excursions and topographical meditations: a day's journey into the counties about London, a visit to the university towns and their colleges and libraries, with their chapels, gardens and memories of the older writers, and the observations of an inland town and its inns and companies of players. A third group are character papers and arguments about books - the pleasures of reading the old poets, the use of a library, the faults of the current criticism, and the portraits of acquaintances and of the peculiar people of the metropolis. The continuing argument is that a retired and obliging temper, reading and remembering, is a sufficient employment for a life without fortune.
narrative_structure: A collection of free-standing essays with no imposed scheme, ordered so that the autobiographical, the topographical and the critical papers alternate; the unity is again that of the persona, whose voice and memory connect the subjects, and the prefactory letter supplies a thin frame for the series.
principal_characters: The essayist writing under the assumed name; the kinsman who professes to edit the papers; the sister of the family history; the collegers and the poor relations; the hostler, the player and the odd characters of the country towns
literary_form: Familiar essay and character sketch, with a share of topographical and university meditation, in the revived Elizabethan and eighteenth-century manner of the first series.
meter_and_prosody: Prose still more various than that of the first series, passing from the gossiping sentence to the long periodic meditation, with a richer and more continuous texture of quotation and with a slower, more elegiac cadence in the retrospective papers.
historical_context: Contributed to the magazines and annuals of the later 1820s and collected in 1833, when the writer had withdrawn from his official employment and had taken a late literary independence; the university and country papers belong to the tour-writing of the 1830s, and the volume appeared in the same years as the first collected editions of the essays in the periodical press.
literary_significance: Completes the series that defined the English familiar essay of the nineteenth century, and contains papers, among them the university excursion and the later country essays, that are usually placed beside the best of the first series. The two volumes together remain the standard model of the personal essay, and this series is the document of the essayist's old age and of his last quarrels and kindnesses.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the prefatory letter, which affects to proceed from a relation of the earlier writer, is by the same hand, and the periodicals of first appearance for the several papers are recorded in the collected editions.
bibliographical_notes: First collected London, 1833, the papers having appeared in magazines and annuals during the later 1820s; it was afterwards joined to the first series in the collected editions, of which the earliest joint issue appeared in the years following the author's death.

title: Tales from Shakespeare
alternative_titles: Tales from Shakespeare. Written for the Young Folks who love their Books, but have not leisure to read all the Plays themselves
description: A collection of prose retellings of twenty of the plays, issued in 1807 in two volumes and written for young readers by two brothers and sisters of one family, with the elder's hand chiefly in the preface and in some of the histories and the younger's in the greater number of the tales. The volume tells the comedies and tragedies as stories, keeping much of the original dialogue in its narrative, and it has been the ordinary introduction to the plays for children in English for two centuries.
plot_or_argument: The tales follow the plays in a single continuous narrative each, abridging the sub-plot and explaining the characters rather than arguing about them. The volumes open with the tale of the storm-raising enchanter and the recovered dukedom, and pass through the comedy of twins separated, the comedies of error and of mistaken identity, the pastoral and romantic comedies, the histories of the English kings, and the great tragedies of revenge, jealousy and ambition, ending with the tale of the tempest, the injured Duke and the renounced magic. Each narrative retains the words of the original wherever they can be given without difficulty, so that the child's first knowledge of the plays is of phrases still belonging to the plays themselves; the moral commentary is light, and the interest is the story, the wonder and the pathos.
narrative_structure: Twenty independent prose tales, one to each play, arranged in two volumes with no continuous frame; the method is a plain narrative voice, with dialogue transcribed or paraphrased, and with the supernatural and the comic elements preserved in their original strangeness.
principal_characters: The figures of the plays retold in prose, including the twins of the comedy of errors, the merchant and the heiress of the comedy, the star-crossed children of the tragedy of Verona, the Scottish thane and his wife, the wronged Duke of the melancholy comedy, and the injured Duke of the last romance with his spirit and his abjured art
literary_form: Juvenile retelling of dramatic romance in prose, a children's anthology that adapts the stage for the reading of the young and holds the sentence structure of the original within a plain narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of great simplicity, in short declarative sentences for the child's ear, with the quoted lines of the plays set in their own rhythm inside the narrative; the style is deliberately free of the moralising manner of much children's book-writing of the day.
historical_context: Written and published in London in 1807, in the years when the family of the writers was established in literary work and when the plays were being widely acted and read; it belonged to the growing trade in books for the young, and its companion volume of educational tales by the same household had already made the authors' names familiar to publishers.
literary_significance: The most durable children's book of the Romantic period and for most English readers the first entrance into the plays; its retellings fixed a canon of the plays for young readers and are still in print. It is also the most widely read work to which a woman of the period contributed the larger share, and its joint authorship has been a standing case in discussions of collaborative and unattributed women's writing.
attribution_notes: Jointly written, with the division of labour variously reported; the customary account assigns the greater part of the tales to the younger member of the household and a smaller share, with the preface, to the elder, and the evidence is the family correspondence and the later statements of the survivors rather than any contemporaneous record of the partition.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1807, in two volumes, in a small octavo series for children, with a frontispiece, the title page giving the authors only as the writers of a former volume of stories for young persons; a companion series of tales from the same plays, and many school editions, followed in the nineteenth century.

title: Characters of Shakespeare's Plays
alternative_titles: Characters of Shakespear's Plays
description: The first of the author's books of criticism, published in 1817, a series of essays on the principal plays which is at once a defence of poetry and imagination against abstract morality and the most influential English book of Shakespearean character-criticism of its century. Its method is to read each play as a succession of minds, argued from the speeches themselves and from the effect of the plays on the stage and in the imagination, and its governing claim is that the dramatist's poetry is a poetry of character and feeling rather than of plot or of instruction.
plot_or_argument: The opening essay states the principle that the author's characters are not specimens of a class but individual creations, and that to judge the plays by rules of criticism or by a moral account is to miss the reason they please. Successive papers take the tragedies and the comedies in turn: the doubting and self-analysing prince of the Danish court, whose hesitation is a disease of the reflective mind and not a defect of the plot; the Moor, whose jealousy is a jealous and credulous nature wrought upon by art; the king divided between his daughters and the flatterers about him; the Macbeth hurried to guilt by a will that is at once his own and another's, with the queen who unmakes her sex; and the comedies, with their fools, their persons of pomp and their women of spirit, and the sentimental and the cynical characters of the earlier plays. The argument throughout is that the poet's gift was an imaginative sympathy which entered into every mind and was nothing exclusively itself, and that criticism of the plays should be a report of the passion and the character as they are felt.
narrative_structure: A series of free-standing essays, one to each of some twenty plays, with a general introduction and a concluding paper on the plays of the earlier and later manner; there is no historical or chronological design, and the order is that of the critic's own argument about the faculties of the poet.
principal_characters: The figures of the plays discussed - the Danish prince, the Moor of Venice, the learned king and his daughters, thane and lady of the Scottish play, the women of the comedies, the fools, the persons of state and the men of fancy
literary_form: Character-writing and practical criticism of the drama, in the line of the Elizabethan book of characters and of the periodical essay, applied to a repertory of plays and to the theory of imaginative sympathy.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the most forceful and compressed kind, full of pointed antithesis, of short sentences of assertion and of long periods of accumulation, with quotation woven into the argument; the style itself is a model of English critical prose.
historical_context: Published in 1817, when the old drama was being revived on the London stage and when the poet's contemporaries, the lecturers and the editors, were making a new profession of literary criticism; the book grew out of papers contributed to periodicals and was written in the years of the author's work as a reporter and as a reviewer for the leading journals.
literary_significance: The foundation of modern character-based Shakespeare criticism and the book by which the plays were read by the nineteenth century for their minds rather than for their scheme; its essays on the great tragedies are still quoted as the classic statements of the imaginative and sympathetic method. It also fixed the reputation of its author as the first critic of the Romantic period.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1817, in a single octavo volume, and reissued in the author's lifetime and after his death in the collected editions; it was followed by the printed lectures of 1818 and 1819, and the several texts are recorded in the standard modern edition of the criticism.

title: Lectures on the English Poets
description: A course of five lectures on the English poets, delivered in the early months of 1818 before a subscribers' institution in London and printed in the same year. The lectures trace the poetry of the nation from the Elizabethans to the living writers, on the principle that poetry is the language of the imagination and of passion, and they are at once a history, a theory and a quarrel with the criticism of the day.
plot_or_argument: The first lecture states the general argument: poetry is not a matter of taste or of rule but of the passions and the imagination, and it arises from a sense of the power of the mind over its objects. The following lectures pass over the period in a sequence of portraits: the Elizabethan drama and its great contemporaries, with their abundance and their want of system; the poet of the paradise lost, whose sublimity is that of a mind conversant with the terrible and the great; the age of the couplet and of the school of polish, with the strength and the limits of its satire and its didactic verse; and the romantic and the modern poets, among them the living writers of the Lake school, the poet of the Oriental tales, and the younger revolutionary singers. The lectures estimate each by the degree of imagination found in them, praise the passion of the old drama, and argue that the age of criticism and of the couplet has lost something of the poetry of the imagination.
narrative_structure: Five delivered lectures, printed much as they were spoken, with an opening lecture of principle and four of historical succession; the design is critical rather than narrative, and the portraits are linked by the recurring distinction between imagination and mechanical ingenuity.
literary_form: Lectures on the history and theory of poetry, in the Romantic critical manner, combining the portrait essay, the historical survey and the argument about the faculties.
meter_and_prosody: Spoken prose, with the period built for the ear, the frequent antithesis, the abrupt sentence of judgment, and the long accumulation of illustration that distinguishes a lecture from an essay.
historical_context: Delivered at a London institution for the diffusion of knowledge in the spring of 1818, in the season of public lecture courses and of the new profession of the man of letters, and printed the same year by a publisher of the lecture series; the course followed the author's first book of dramatic criticism and preceded the lectures of the following year on the comic writers.
