literary_significance: A shaping book of the Romantic history of poetry, influential in fixing the canon and in the vocabulary by which English verse was judged for the next century, and the classic statement of the doctrine that poetry is the speech of imagination and passion. Its portraits of the Elizabethans and of the poet of the lost Paradise, and its account of the living poets of its own day, are still standard quotations in the history of criticism.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Delivered and first published London, 1818, in a single volume of the institution's lecture series, and reprinted in the collected editions of the criticism, with the later revisions recorded; translations and American reprintings followed within the same decade.

title: Lectures on the English Comic Writers
description: A course of lectures on the English writers of humour and satire, delivered in 1819 and printed in the same year, which together with the lectures of the previous year made its author the historian of English prose as well as of English poetry. Its argument is that humour is a moral and social faculty, that it requires a sense of the absurd arising from self-love and from the contradictions of manners, and that the great comic writers are serious men who have turned their observation of themselves and of the world upon its mistakes.
plot_or_argument: The opening lecture distinguishes humour from wit and from satire, and makes the laugh of the comic writer a product of contrast and of the unexpected, with a constant reference to the sense of power that laughter gives. The following lectures take the writers in a loose succession: the essayists and character-writers of the Elizabethan age and their humours, the comic drama of the Restoration and its picture of manners, the writers of the spectator papers with their politeness and their moral machinery, the novelist and romancer of the same school, the greater humorist of the century who satirised learning and dulness, the philosopher of humour and his theory of the laughable, and the novelists and essayists of the author's own day. The argument runs through the whole that the best humour has its seat in a tenderness and a self-forgetfulness which the mere satirist wants, and that the age of good humour is an age of ease and of good nature rather than of struggle.
narrative_structure: Four delivered lectures, printed as spoken, with a general lecture of principle and three of historical succession, the several writers grouped rather than systematised, and with digressions on the theory of laughter and on the state of contemporary letters.
literary_form: Lectures on the history of prose humour and satire, in the Romantic critical manner, combining the theory of laughter with the portrait and the historical survey.
meter_and_prosody: Lecture prose of an easy and discursive kind, with the period built for the ear and a frequent use of the illustrative quotation and of the short verdict; the style is less weighty than that of the lectures on the poets and more conversational.
historical_context: Delivered and published in London in 1819, in the season of the lecture institutions and of the new market for printed criticism, following the lectures on the poets of the previous year and preceding those on the drama of the Elizabethan age; the book takes in the controversy about the theory of the laughable then current from the older essays.
literary_significance: The first English history of comic prose as a serious subject and a standard authority for the reading of the essayists, the character-writers and the novelists of humour; its definitions of humour, wit and satire long held place in handbooks of the subject. It also fixed the canon of English prose for later schoolmen and is a central document of the Romantic essay's account of itself.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Delivered and first published London, 1819, in a volume of the lecture series issued from the institution at which the course was given; reprinted in the collected editions, and separately edited for schools in the later nineteenth century.

title: Lectures on the Dramatic Literature of the Age of Elizabeth
alternative_titles: Lectures, Chiefly on the Dramatic Literature of the Age of Elizabeth
description: The third course of printed lectures, delivered and published in 1820, on the drama of the Elizabethan and Jacobean age, and the author's most concentrated book on the theatre. It argues that the drama of that age lived by the sense of character and of passion, by novelty of situation and by the sympathy of a mixed audience, and it opposes to the criticism that measures plays by rule a defence of the irregular abundance of the stage of the playhouses.
plot_or_argument: The first lecture states the general character of the age, its mixture of the tragic and the comic, its freedom from the rules, and the conditions of the public theatre that produced it. The lectures that follow give a succession of portraits of the dramatists of the period before and after the great poet of the age: the university wits and their learning, the writers of city comedy and of the humours, the writers of civic and of domestic tragedy, the romancist of the stage and his sensitive and moralised plays, the satirist of the court and his strength and his meanness, and the poet of the later plays whose dialogue and whose scenes of suffering are placed with honour beside the greater masters. Against these the author sets the French and the classical model, and the argument concludes that the true test of the drama is not its observance of the rules but its power over the imagination and its passion of character.
narrative_structure: Five delivered lectures, one of general account of the age and four of succession of dramatists, with a closing comparison between the national drama and the regulated stage of the Continent; the plan is critical and historical rather than narrative.
literary_form: Lectures on the history of the drama, combining the portrait of the playwright, the account of the stage and its conditions, and the argument about the rules.
meter_and_prosody: Lecture prose of a vigorous and summary kind, with short sentences of judgment balanced against long periods of description, and frequent quotation from the plays discussed.
historical_context: Delivered and published in London in 1820, in the years of the revivals of the old drama on the nineteenth-century stage and of the new attention to the unrevised plays and the accounts of the players; the course followed the lectures on the poets and on the comic writers, and was issued from the institution that had engaged the lecturer.
literary_significance: The book that shaped the modern estimate of the secondary dramatists of the age of the national theatre, and a foundation of the historical study of the Elizabethan stage; its portraits long stood as the standard introduction to the writers it discusses. Its defence of the irregular drama against rule is the most complete statement of the Romantic case for the older English stage.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested.
bibliographical_notes: Delivered at a London institution for the diffusion of knowledge and first published London, 1820, in a single volume; a second edition with revisions followed within the next year, and the text is reprinted in the collected editions of the criticism.

title: The Spirit of the Age
alternative_titles: The Spirit of the Age; or, Contemporary Portraits
description: A series of contemporary portraits published in 1825 and usually taken to be its author's best book, which gives the name of the age to a collection of critical and political characters. Its plan is to read the mind of the time through a series of individuals, poets, essayists, critics, advocates, statesmen and men of science and of the church, each essay treating its subject as the exponent of a habit of mind rather than as a private person. The book is at once the most acute record of English literature in the 1820s and a specimen of the character-writing revived by the Romantic essayists.
plot_or_argument: The preface argues that a great age of literature may be recognised by its dominant habits of mind, and that the present is an age of discussion, of personality and of transition. The portraits of the poets of the northern lakes, of the poet of abstraction and of the writer of romantic tales are drawn so as to show a poetry of feeling and a poetry of ideas parted from the passion of the public, and the younger and more revolutionary singers are placed under the head of a poetry of motion and of hope. The men of the bar, of the banks, of the church and of the great quarterly journal are given as the characters of an age of enquiry and of party, and the closing papers pass from letters to the arts, with the portrait of the first actor of the London stage and of the one great living painter. Through the whole series the argument is that the age is divided between the spirit of party and the love of the ideal, and that the truest criticism reports the mind of its writer with the same sympathy with which the dramatist reported the minds of his characters.
narrative_structure: A series of some twenty-four independent character-essays, with a general preface on the age and no continuous argument; the unity is that of the method, each paper taking one public figure as the exponent of a habit of mind, and the order being loosely arranged by the divisions of letters, of public affairs and of the arts.
principal_characters: The living writers, critics, pleaders, bankers, statesmen and men of the church and of the stage whose portraits make the series; the essayist himself, who comments on the temper of his own age and on the trade of the literary profession
literary_form: Familiar essay and character sketch in the revived Theophrastan manner, combined with critical review and political character-writing.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the author's most concentrated kind, built of balanced antithesis, of the short sentence of verdict and of the long period of accumulation, with a constant use of the epigrammatic turn and of the summarising clause.
historical_context: Published in London in 1825, several of the papers having appeared during the two preceding years in the magazines, in a season of intellectual and political expectation before the changes in the representation and in the press that followed; the author's own fortunes were at their lowest point, and the portraits of living writers were read as the criticism of a rival and a former friend.
literary_significance: The most quoted book of contemporary portraits in English and the standard account of the literary and intellectual temper of the 1820s, from which most later histories of the period still take their phrases for its poets and its critics. Its method of treating a living writer as the exponent of a habit of mind became the model of the character essay, and its sentences on poetry and on the age are a permanent part of the vocabulary of criticism.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; a second series of portraits, contributed to another journal, appeared some years later and is printed separately in the collected editions.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1825, in a single volume, by a publisher of the literary and radical books of the day, several papers having appeared in magazines in the two preceding years; a second series followed in 1830, and the whole is reprinted in the standard collected edition of the essays and criticism.

title: Table Talk (Hazlitt)
alternative_titles: Table Talk: A Series of Essays
description: A series of essays on the miscellaneous, published in two volumes in 1821 and 1822 and written for the fireside on the model of the talk of a table rather than of a periodical paper. Its subjects are the pleasures and the opinions of a private reader: the love of the old books, the principles of human action and of taste, the differences of town and country, the pleasures of the imagination, travel, the theatre and its great actors, and the history and the quarrels of the age. It is the completest body of its author's familiar prose and one of the classic books of the English essay.
plot_or_argument: The papers have no single thesis but return constantly to a set of oppositions. Several argue that the imagination and not the understanding governs human conduct and opinion, that we are moved by what we hold as an idea rather than by what we know as a fact, and that self-love, with its hope and its fear, is the root of our moral life; one of the earliest papers states this as a philosophy of action, and others apply it to taste, to the love of the great and to the envy that attends it. A second group is the essay of relish: the town and the country and the character of each, the pleasure of reading the old poets, the sound of a stringed instrument, the theatre, a long absence and a return, the luxury of ease, and the use of a library. A third deals with the persons and the quarrels of contemporary literature and politics, pleading the spirit of the age against the cant of the party journals. The whole is bound by the writer's temper, at once eager and indolent, generous and resentful, and by the constant reference of every subject to the act of thinking and feeling in a private mind.
narrative_structure: Two series of short essays, some thirty in all, with no order of matter except the alternation of the philosophical, the descriptive and the critical papers; each piece is a completed meditation, and the unity is that of the voice and of the recurring theory of the imagination.
principal_characters: The essayist at his table; the reader and the idler, the man of town and the dweller in the country; the actors and the authors of the old and of the present drama, and the persons of the literary quarrels of the day
literary_form: Familiar essay and character sketch, with a share of moral philosophy and of critical review, in the line of the table-talk and of the miscellaneous paper.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of remarkable variety, passing from the aphoristic sentence and the sharp paradox to the long and lapping period of the essays on relish, with habitual balance of clause and a frequent use of the negative for emphasis.
historical_context: Written and published in London in 1821 and 1822, when its author was at the height of his critical reputation and before the domestic catastrophe that broke his life, and when the essay, the review and the lecture made a single literary market; the title pages advertise his earlier books of criticism, and the papers were among the first fruits of the profession of letters he had chosen.
literary_significance: One of the canonical books of the English familiar essay, and the storehouse of its author's most repeated papers on the principles of action, on taste and on the pleasures of reading; its essays on the town and the country, on old books and on the actors have been continuously anthologised. Its philosophical papers are also the plainest accessible statement of the theory of the imagination that underlies his criticism.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the bare title is shared with a poem of the same name by a writer of the previous generation and with a later volume of table-talk by a friend and collaborator, and the three are distinguished in libraries by the author's name.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1821 and 1822, in two volumes, the papers having been contributed to a literary monthly magazine, and reissued repeatedly in the collected editions; the volume of 1821 carries the first series and that of 1822 the second, and the order and the originals are recorded in the standard edition.

title: Confessions of an English Opium-Eater
alternative_titles: Confessions of an English Opium-Eater: Taken from an Old Manuscript
description: An autobiographical narrative first published in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in the autumn of 1821 and in book form in London in 1822, giving the account of a young man's years of opium consumption and of the dreams, the terrors and the miseries that it produced. Its matter is the writer's own student life, his flight from his family home, his wandering in Oxford and in the streets of London, his first acquaintance with laudanum as a remedy for bodily pain, and the cascades of dream imagery and of fear that followed, ending with a resolution to moderate but not to abandon the habit. It created the literature of the intoxicating confessional and remains the standard document of opium in English letters.
plot_or_argument: The narrative moves in two parts. The first gives the prehistory of the dreamer's terrors: the death of his mother in his earliest childhood, the tyranny of a schoolmaster at a grammar school in the west, the quarrel with a stern home authority which drove the boy from his family to the lodging of a fellow-student at Oxford, and the weeks of solitary wandering in Oxford and in the streets of London with little money and no protection, in which a friendless outcast girl received such shelter as he could give, and in which opium was first taken as a remedy against bodily suffering. The second part reports the effects of the confirmed habit: the long sleep of some days' duration, the architecture and the populations of the dreams, the mystic stairs and the rooms and the faces without number, the Malay and the persecuting powers, and the recurring sense of space and of eternity in which the hours of sleep became ages. It closes with the account of the bettered and moderated use of the remedy, the plain statement that the writer had no intention of abandoning opium, and the acknowledgement of the consolations and the powers of the faculty which the habit had also given him.
narrative_structure: A first-person confessional in two parts, the prehistory and the dreams, with a closing section on the uses of the remedy; the sequence is chronological in the outer life and associational in the accounts of the dreams, and the book's unity is that of a self examined by its own memory.
principal_characters: The English opium-eater as narrator; his mother, lost in his earliest childhood; the schoolmaster of the grammar school; the stern authority of the broken home; the fellow-student of the Oxford lodging; the friendless girl of the London streets; the Malay and the persecuting forms of the dreams
literary_form: Inward confession and autobiographical prose narrative, combining the memoir, the dream vision and the analytical self-examination in a single confessional form.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of a highly finished and Latinate periodic style, with long accumulating sentences in the passages of terror and short declarative sentences in the moral reflections, and a constant use of parenthesis and of the apostrophe to the reader.
historical_context: Written after the author's settlement in the northern lake country, in the character of a private record of the years of the opium habit, and published in a Scottish monthly magazine in 1821 and in book form in 1822, at a time when the use of opium and laudanum was widely practised and unregulated and when the review journals were the chief vehicle of autobiographical revelation.
literary_significance: The founding text of the literature of intoxication and of the analytic confession in English, and the work that gave the language its vocabulary for the dream and for the pleasure and the terror of the altered mind. Its influence on later confessional writing and on the literature of drugs has been permanent, and it is a standard text for the history of autobiography and of the Romantic study of the mind.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the narrative was published anonymously at first, and the author's later edition of his own works revised and enlarged the text, so that the magazine version of 1821 and the revised book form differ.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in two numbers in the autumn of 1821, and in book form London, 1822, in two volumes, with a title describing the record as taken from an old manuscript; a revised and enlarged version, prefixed to a collection of the author's writings later in the century, is the basis of most modern reprints.

title: Murder as a Fine Art
alternative_titles: On Murder Considered with Reference to its Pleasures
description: A prose essay published in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in 1827, which treats the pleasures of murder as a branch of aesthetic criticism and is one of the most quoted pieces of English ironic prose. Under cover of a paper read to a club of connoisseurs, the writer argues that murder, duly considered as a fine art, has its rules, its pleasures and its properly aesthetic critics, and he reviews the celebrated cases of the day in the manner of a connoisseur discussing a picture. The leisurely ironic argument is its machinery, and the exposure of the reader's appetite for the dreadful is the point of the performance.
plot_or_argument: The essay opens with the complaint that, whatever has been written on the agreeable, the beautiful and the sublime, murder has been left out of the catalogue of the fine arts, and proposes to supply the deficiency. A paper is therefore read before a club of amateurs, which distinguishes the kinds and the circumstances of murder, requires the true critic to read the case with the feelings of a connoisseur, and rebukes the public that will not attend to the pleasure of the thing. The body of the essay is a review of recent notorious cases and of their trials and reporting, in which the narrator criticises the paragraph writers and the jurymen, complains that the murders of the metropolis are unattended by taste and that the age has lost the relish for the art, and lays down the proper method for the future conduct of a murder, including the choice of subject, of season and of place and the arrangement for the amusement of the reader. The argument closes with a promise of a second paper, and its effect is a satire on the readers of the new police reporting and on the aesthetic criticism of the agreeable.
narrative_structure: A single free-standing essay in the form of a paper read to a club, with an opening statement of principles, a review of the cases and a closing promise of a sequel; the irony is sustained by the perfect good humour of the narrator, who never breaks the character of the connoisseur.
principal_characters: The narrator, a connoisseur and member of the club of amateurs; the members of the club who hear the paper; the reporters, the jurymen and the public of the metropolis whose taste is criticised; the sufferers and the criminals of the notorious cases reviewed
literary_form: Ironical critical essay and prose satire, applying the vocabulary of aesthetic taste to a subject from which it is repulsive, in the manner of the ironical project and of the club oration.
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the urbane and deliberate kind, with long periods, parenthesis, the language of the club and of the pulpit, and an unfailing courtesy of tone that carries the irony.
historical_context: Published in the same Edinburgh monthly that had first printed the author's confessions of an intoxication, in a season of popular interest in criminal trial and in the reporting of the new police; the piece belongs to the London journalism of the later 1820s and to the controversy about the taste and the morals of the periodical press.
literary_significance: The most famous essay in English on the aesthetic treatment of horror and a permanent source of the phrase and the notion it parodies; it established the model of the ironical critical sketch that later writers of prose virtuosity have imitated. It remains a standard text for the study of Romantic irony, of the literature of crime and of the periodical press, and its title was adopted for the collected edition of the author's papers on the subject.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; a second paper of the same design followed in a later year and is printed with this one in the collected edition from which the title used here is taken.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in 1827; the papers on the subject were collected under the title used here in the author's edition of his own writings later in the century, and the magazine text is recorded in the standard edition of the works.
